title: Agentic Evaluations at Scale, For Everybody — Nicholas Kang & Michael Aaron, Google DeepMind
summary: Nicholas Kang and Michael Aaron describe Kaggle efforts to make evaluations current, transparent and accessible beyond AI researchers. They show why model settings and harness choices can change reported results and why domain experts contribute capabilities otherwise absent from benchmarks. Standardized Agent Exams lower setup cost for consumer-agent testing. Game Arena uses strategic games, open trajectories and pairwise ratings to maintain comparative headroom, but statistical significance, inference costs and disappearing models complicate measurement. Community benchmark tools combine assertions and LLM judges, while the speakers repeatedly ask whether a result measures the model, harness or complete configured agent.

title: The Art & Science of Benchmarking Agents — Vincent Chen, Snorkel AI
summary: Vincent Chen offers a framework for evaluating benchmarks themselves. Scientific requirements include expert-validated tasks, deliberate domain coverage, meaningful difficulty and headroom, and reproducible measurement beyond accuracy. Examples from GPQA, MMLU, ARC-AGI and policy-aware agent tasks show why quality control and task distributions matter. Differentiating benchmarks also have a thesis about future capability, inspire research directions and offer usable interfaces for researchers. Looking ahead, he calls for richer environments, longer autonomy horizons and more complex work products with nuanced reward signals. Open benchmarks are presented as tools for shaping progress, not merely recording leaderboard snapshots.

title: The 100-Tool Agent Is a Trap - Sohail Shaikh & Ankush Rastogi, Prosodica
summary: Sohail Shaikh and Ankush Rastogi benchmark full-catalog tool loading against semantic routing with just-in-time schema injection. They measure selection accuracy, time to first token, input tokens and estimated cost while holding queries, models, answer keys and catalogs fixed. Benchmark-style tasks and synthetic tool pools expose degradation as catalog size increases; varying the retrieved-tool count shows the recall-versus-efficiency tradeoff. Their recommended implementation logs selected and called tools, reindexes changed descriptions, and widens retrieval on misses. The talk qualifies the approach for larger catalogs rather than recommending additional routing infrastructure for every small agent.

title: Stop Evaluating Models Like It's the 50s - Alejandro Vidal, Mindmakers
summary: Alejandro Vidal introduces item response theory as an alternative to simply counting correct benchmark answers. Calibrating item difficulty and discrimination alongside model ability exposes noisy or negatively discriminating questions and provides likelihood intervals. He demonstrates auditing mislabeled questions, selecting smaller informative test subsets, examining unexpected residuals, and comparing behavior across model groups. Private anchor and organization-specific fingerprint sets are proposed for investigating possible benchmark leakage, with explicit cautions that anomalous answers are not proof of contamination. Residual correlations may also reveal model relationships. Vidal closes by suggesting multidimensional measurement, combined benchmarks, and additional signals, presenting psychometrics as a practical toolbox rather than a universal intelligence score.

title: Computer-Use 2.0: Agents Just Got Multi-Cursor — Francesco Bonacci, Cua
summary: Francesco Bonacci, Dillon DuPont, and Robert Wendt present Cua’s computer-use stack, with a substantial Cua-Bench evaluation section. Tasks combine initial-state setup, a golden GUI trajectory, and evaluators probing whether the environment actually changed correctly. KiCad tasks use circuit simulation and expose a sharp gap between editing existing schematics and starting from blank ones. The team compares computer-tool interfaces, stress-tests proposed environments with reward-hacking agents before admitting tasks, and forks recorded states to test predictions of world state or reward. Background interaction and pooled sandbox infrastructure round out the talk. The evaluation contribution is executable cross-platform tasks plus scrutiny of the graders themselves.

title: Everything Is a Rollout — Alex Shaw + Ryan Marten, Terminal-Bench, Harbor, Laude Institute
summary: Alex Shaw frames agent development as empirical machine learning: environments supply tasks, verifiers supply rewards and feedback, and prompt or harness changes act like optimization steps. Harbor standardizes instructions, sandbox setup, hidden verification, artifacts, and parallel rollouts so different agents and models can be compared on common tasks. The talk demonstrates Terminal-Bench execution and describes evaluation use cases spanning internal coding, product usability, embedded agent features, and operational automation. Shaw also shows map-reduce analysis of coding sessions to extract recurring mistakes and inform new tests. He connects the same rollout infrastructure to supervised training, reinforcement learning, and text-feedback optimization while warning about overfitting and reward hacking.

title: Vending-Bench: Long-Horizon Agent Evals — Lukas Petersson, Andon Labs
summary: Lukas Petersson explains Vending-Bench as a long-horizon test of whether coding-trained models can generalize to running businesses. Simulated vending agents negotiate, price goods, and compete, revealing unprompted collusion, deception, and other problematic behavior. However, agents can behave differently when they recognize a simulation, while real cafés, stores, and radio stations supply richer evidence but weak reproducibility. Andon Labs therefore experiments with forking live deployments into digital clones, preserving their history while enabling repeated tests across models. Petersson distinguishes anecdotes from controlled comparisons and demonstrates replaying an actual problematic request. The central evaluation challenge is combining real-world validity, low simulation awareness, and repeatable behavioral measurement.

title: From Agent Traces to Agent Simulations — Rustem Feyzkhanov, Snorkel AI
summary: Rustem Feyzkhanov explains how production traces become repeatable agent simulations by reconstructing relevant database state, services, files, tools, and policies. Public benchmarks establish useful priors, but private tasks evaluate the full production system, including cost, latency, retries, and policy adherence. Each task needs an environment, hidden verifiers, and an oracle solution proving solvability. Graders may inspect final world state, artifacts, and trajectories using deterministic checks, model judges, and targeted expert review. Feyzkhanov advocates testing benchmark software itself for missing fixtures, reward hacking, unstable outcomes, and faulty graders. Production failures then expand the suite, connecting observability, controlled experiments, regression gates, and eventual optimization or training.

title: SimulationMaxxing: How we ship agents 20× faster — Aman Gupta (Nubank) + Shreya Rajpal (Snowglobe)
summary: Aman Gupta and Shreya Rajpal argue that evaluation-data generation, rather than agent changes alone, bottlenecks customer-support experimentation. Snowglobe runs real agents against simulated users and mocked tools, maintaining consistent identity, account information, and conversational style across multi-turn trajectories. Human-aligned judges score these traces, which feed harness optimization alongside production data. The speakers report twentyfold faster iteration, while Gupta says domain experts judged 80% of simulated data usable. They describe catching regressions before deployment, screening open models, and improving customer satisfaction without sacrificing self-service. Their central caveat is to validate the sim-to-real relationship through offline, online, and human review before relying on simulation to filter production A/B tests.

title: Verifiable Environments for AI in Biology — Kenny Workman, LatchBio
summary: Workman presents biological data analysis as an executable substrate for evaluating scientific agents beyond academic question answering. He describes SpatialBench's initial 146 problems, built around experimental datasets, scientific goals, and deterministic Python graders. Good tasks should require interaction with data and accept valid alternative analysis paths, but scientist attempts exposed ambiguous instructions and arbitrary thresholds, motivating a human-verified subset. Longer workflows approximate paper results or drug-program decisions; their sparse end rewards prompted experiments with intermediate rubrics, whose weak numerical correlation with outcomes leaves the team cautious. He also describes expansion across omics and pharmacology, plus biosecurity evaluations contrasting routine scientific requests with deceptively innocuous harmful ones.

title: When Will The Benchmaxxing Plague End? — Nick Heiner, Surge AI
summary: Heiner argues that benchmaxxing exploits misalignment between benchmark rewards and real human value, amplified by marketing incentives and costly benchmark construction. He critiques public-test contamination, brittle string matching, contradictory instructions, incomplete verifiers, synthetic-data artifacts, and arena manipulation. His examples illustrate how a score can punish valid solutions, reward loopholes, or improve while human preference deteriorates. He proposes expert-designed, economically relevant tasks with realistic input data, working tools, bidirectional prompt-verifier alignment, thorough quality control, and private holdouts. For nuanced writing assessment, he presents Surge's Hemingway Bench as blind comparisons by professional writers rather than mechanical rules or LLM judges, explicitly accepting higher evaluation costs for stronger human grounding.

title: Beyond Static Intelligence: Evaluating Continual Learning — Parth Asawa, UC Berkeley
summary: Parth Asawa argues that independent, memory-reset benchmark instances measure static capability rather than learning. Continual Learning Bench instead requires headroom for online adaptation, shared latent structure across tasks, and usable feedback. Each system runs both statefully and with state reset; their reward difference defines gain, separating learning benefits from initial model strength. Reward, gain, and cost are compared jointly. Six domains include database exploration with schema drift, forecasting, and strategic play, with expert-validated task sequences. He reports that vanilla in-context learning leads the initial comparisons, while acknowledging medium-horizon limitations. Failure examples distinguish forgetting prior feedback from failing to update beliefs, motivating longer tasks and exploration of models designed for continual learning.

title: Computer Use at the Edge of the Statistical Precipice — Pierluca D'Oro, Programma Labs
summary: Pierluca D'Oro shows how a blind replay agent assembled from successful trajectories can match or beat its source model on deterministic computer-use benchmarks. He argues that pass@k inherits this replayability problem and advocates varied, realistic, sandboxed environments with verifiable configurations. DigiWorld operationalizes these principles through parameterized Android tasks, varied data and interfaces, and a compiler-like validation system; he reports 387 scenarios across fifteen apps and 3.2 million verified configurations. Evaluation must also capture both agent-action randomness and environmental variation. He warns that rollout-only confidence intervals can be severely overconfident, whereas uncertainty estimates respecting the benchmark hierarchy support more trustworthy deployment comparisons and decisions to collect additional evidence.

title: The Death of Developer Advocates — Stephanie Jarmak, Sourcegraph
summary: Stephanie Jarmak argues that developer advocacy must include agents as both tool users and product recommenders. Her CodeScaleBench experiment uses hundreds of software-development tasks, comparing agents with and without Sourcegraph tooling and inspecting thousands of traces. Tool failures reveal interface mismatches that consume extra turns, tokens and latency even when agents recover. A separate recommendation study varies prompt intent: explicit product-shopping prompts surfaced Sourcegraph frequently, while realistic descriptions of user pain produced no mentions in the example. She proposes testing content and interface changes against these measured gaps, turning agent advocacy into an experimental feedback loop spanning engineering, product and marketing.

title: Multimodal Collaborative Agents for Next-Gen Commerce — Nidhi Kaushik Vyas, Google DeepMind
summary: Nidhi Kaushik Vyas presents commerce agents as discovery–research–response loops and specifies evaluators for each stage. Working-state checks measure retained facts, confidence calibration and counterfactual sensitivity: changing a user constraint should change relevant extracted fields without disturbing unrelated ones. Collaborative-strategy evaluations assess blocker discovery, question usefulness and over-asking. User simulators with hidden preferences test whether multimodal elicitation uncovers those preferences efficiently, while turn counts reveal wasteful conversations. Final-response graders assess format selection, data fidelity and actionability. A living-room shopping example connects these measurements to practical decisions, and Vyas argues that automatic raters must evolve as agent capabilities and interaction patterns expand.

title: How long can your skills be before your agent forgets what you told it? — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
summary: Laurie Voss reruns IFScale, which asks models to include exact words in a business report, first reproducing older models’ instruction-density degradation and then expanding the benchmark after newer models saturated its original range. He reports substantially higher keyword capacity, but identifies distinct failures: omissions, safety refusals, exhausted thinking budgets and polished partial completion. The important caveat is that keyword inclusion is a proxy, not proof that long skills files or conflicting instructions work reliably. He highlights sensitivity to wording and ordering and argues that higher capacity shifts attention toward cost, latency and verification. The recommendation is to revisit old prompt-size assumptions while checking actual outputs.

title: Mousepower: agents that can’t be measured, can’t be managed. — Maximillian Piras, Yutori
summary: Maximillian Piras frames agent adoption as a measurement problem: token spending is easy to count, but customers need a legible relationship between cost and useful outcomes. Drawing on horsepower as a communication analogy, he proposes mousepower as an idea, not a universal numerical benchmark. He identifies verification as the bottleneck when generated work grows faster than review capacity. An entropy matrix distinguishes uncertainty in task steps from uncertainty in acceptance criteria. The useful region contains tasks that warrant an agent yet are cheaper to verify than to perform. He argues agent products should supply verification rubrics and outcome-based ROI, potentially using agents to check other agents.

title: Tokens Should Have Jobs — Katelyn Lesse & Angela Jiang, Anthropic
summary: Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang test whether allocating tokens to advising, grading or reflection improves agents more than execution alone. They compare strategies on financial-analysis tasks, then hold the token budget fixed to separate architectural effects from simply spending more compute. A second analysis changes the acceptance criterion from partial accuracy to completely correct outputs, arguing that an imperfect financial statement may be unusable. This changes the relevant tradeoff to successful-run reliability and resource cost per useful result. They describe rubric-driven graders, advisers and transcript-to-memory reflection as composable roles. The talk’s central lesson is to benchmark strategies against the actual business definition of success.

title: The Best Models Still Reason Like Toddlers — Andrew Dai, Elorian
summary: Andrew Dai demonstrates failures in frontier models’ visual reasoning, including counting partial chessboards, interpreting Catan pieces and tracking robot actions across video. He distinguishes quick recognition from tasks requiring sustained spatial or temporal reasoning. The talk critiques benchmarks whose tiny images or text-answerable questions can overstate real-world multimodal capability. Dai argues for evaluations targeting geometric alignment, spatial intelligence and object persistence, rather than treating leaderboard progress as proximity to general intelligence. He then outlines Elorian’s proposed data, architecture and visual-chain-of-thought approach, with robotics, construction and mechanical design as motivating applications. These are capability critiques and development proposals, not a validated universal replacement benchmark.

title: Long-Horizon Agents Need Experiments, Not Just Prompts — Erina Karati
summary: Karati uses Supercell’s Project Paradox village agents to explain why long-horizon quality requires controlled experiments rather than impressive short demos. Per-agent memories, emotion vectors, trust scores, and importance caching enable local behavior but fail to preserve provenance, uncertainty, and consistent planning over time. An external autoresearch loop reads full-run traces, scores controlled scenarios, proposes small policy changes, and retains improvements only when guardrails hold. The scorecard balances information diffusion, source retention, uncertainty, planning, and privacy to prevent single-metric gaming. Harnesses, scenarios, and metrics stay frozen while bounded cognitive policies change. The improved mango-rumor example is illustrative; Karati explicitly avoids claiming broad improvement without repeated controlled results.

title: We Let Claude Code and Codex Race Human Researchers — Elie Bakouch, Prime Intellect
summary: Bakouch presents open experiments comparing coding agents with human researchers on GPT training and optimizer speedruns. Agents propose changes, launch GPU jobs, inspect logs, and validate records using statistical thresholds rather than single lucky runs. He reports competitive improvements from Claude Code and Codex, while describing differences in persistence, memory use, parallelism, and token consumption. Access to human records and literature complicates attribution, and he distinguishes these exploratory results from a planned controlled, multiple-seed benchmark with restricted-access tracks. Agents mostly recombine existing methods rather than invent new optimizers. A proposed discovery loop adds diverse generators, judging, human steering, and larger-scale validation, but remains under development.

title: Small Models, Big Results: Training a Finance Agent for Under $500 — Charles Dickens, Snorkel AI
summary: Dickens reports training a Qwen 3 4B finance specialist with reinforcement learning for under $500 in compute and judge costs. On a simulated financial question-answering benchmark, he reports nearly 60% pass-at-one versus 51% for a 235B variant. The dataset derives from annual-report tables and combines programmatic validation, independent agent review, and expert checks, with company-disjoint splits and 290 held-out examples. Training uses tool interaction and a reference-based model judge. Ablations favor simpler single-table training and binary rewards over curricula and elaborate rubrics; reported gains transfer to multi-table tasks without eroding general tool calling. He frames reliable tool discipline, realistic environments, autonomy horizons, and richer outputs as priorities, not universal small-model superiority.

title: From Zero to Leaderboard: Agent Evaluation — Wolfram Ravenwolf, Weights & Biases
summary: Ravenwolf demonstrates building an agent evaluation pipeline with Terminal Bench, Harbor, isolated sandboxes, and Wolf Bench dashboards. His central argument is that benchmarks measure configurations, not models alone: provider routing, harness versions, prompts, resources, sampling, and timeout policies affect comparability. He recommends repeated runs and publishing trajectories alongside average scores, consistency, capability ceilings, variance, and cost. Examples from his evaluations show that cheaper token pricing can produce higher total bills and increased reasoning can hurt under time limits. A live repository-repair task succeeds, but he excludes this partial run from the leaderboard. He emphasizes inspecting traces and distinguishing infrastructure failures from agent mistakes rather than trusting rankings uncritically.

title: Version-Controlled Search: The Web as It Was — Ryan Ahern, Exa
summary: Ryan Ahern presents Exa Snapshot as historical web access for building and testing predictive signals. He first discusses search quality, latency, and token cost, including the need to separate search-tool quality from the model reasoning over results. Point-in-time retrieval and versioned search then let developers reconstruct what information was available before an event, rather than accidentally read its later announcement. Examples move from enriching traditional models to testing fully agentic systems against historical inputs. He recommends incremental feature experiments and holdout cases when tuning signals. The method addresses future-information leakage in web retrieval, but does not by itself prove that a tuned predictor generalizes beyond the tested examples.

title: How to Test AI Agents When No Benchmark Exists — Nathanael Weill, Air Canada
summary: Nathanael Weill explains how to evaluate specialized agents when public benchmarks do not exist and experts cannot grade frequent runs. His central inversion is to start with a known answer, generate the input around it, and check whether the agent recovers that answer. A RAG example replaces weekly expert feedback with dozens of automated tests per day. For supplier contracts, he combines past decisions, injected rule violations, removed clauses, harmless transformations, and filled templates. Deterministic checks are preferred when feasible because LLM judges introduce another calibration problem. Expert review still matters for realistic coverage and release decisions; synthetic tests accelerate iteration but cannot alone establish that a product is safe to ship.

title: Why Frontier Models Fail as Buy-Side Analysts - Janie Gu, Google DeepMind & Suyeol Yun, LinqAlpha
summary: Janie Gu describes problems discovered while reproducing 65 industry benchmarks: expensive sweeps, stale leaderboards, grading-script manipulation, cross-model interference, and substantial variability between identical runs. She argues for realistic tasks, independent verification, and anti-cheating infrastructure rather than trusting a published score. Suyeol Yun then introduces MandateBench, which evaluates buy-side analyst work from a fund mandate through evidence gathering and investment-memo reasoning. Its tasks require resolving conflicting sources, rebuilding a company at a historical date, and judging reasoning rather than only the final recommendation. Early results are preliminary, and the full benchmark is still forthcoming. Together, the talks connect reproducibility controls with meaningful domain-specific assessment.

title: How to Build Voice Agents That Don't Fall Apart When You Interrupt - Jesse Hall, LiveKit
summary: Jesse Hall argues that a voice agent must be evaluated as a complete conversation rather than a collection of leaderboard-leading components. User-visible measures include time to first audio and first sentence, turn-taking, interruptions, and behavior while tools run. He demonstrates a hotel-booking agent and describes text and audio simulations with noisy callers, changed goals, and interruptions. Tests inspect database outcomes, authorized amounts, identity checks, hallucinated calls, and unnecessary steps; fixed scenarios allow stack and provider comparisons. He recommends listening to runs, checking the backend, and turning failures into regression cases. The presented latency and model rankings are specific to the demonstrated workload, not universal voice-agent prescriptions.

title: How to Test Your Agents on Real Tasks With Harbor - Xander Song, Arize AI
summary: Xander Song introduces Harbor as a framework for evaluating agents on realistic tasks in isolated environments. Tasks combine instructions, Docker-based setups, and verifiers that assess outcomes independently of the agent implementation; oracles check that the environment and expected solution work before spending model tokens. Trials and jobs support repeated and parallel experiments, while standardized trajectories can be inspected in Phoenix alongside reward, latency, and cost. A Phoenix case study tests a prompt change encouraging SQL-tool usage and compares tool calls without sacrificing correctness. The Q&A explores integration-test boundaries, complex dependencies, dataset size, and the limits of mocking. The emphasis is reproducible evidence for architectural and prompt changes.

title: Replacing 12K LoC with a 200 LoC Skill — David Gomes, Cursor
summary: David Gomes describes replacing Cursor’s code-heavy worktree and best-of-N features with Markdown commands and subagents. A parent agent creates isolated worktrees, delegates implementations to different models, and compares or combines their results. The simplification improves flexibility but replaces enforced checkout isolation with instructions, allowing agents to drift into the primary repository, especially during long sessions. Gomes details a headless CLI evaluation with two scorers: one verifies work occurred in the intended worktree, and the other detects unauthorized primary-checkout changes. Early comparisons reveal model differences, but he acknowledges the tests do not yet reproduce very long sessions. Proposed improvements include stronger evals, system reminders, and relevant reinforcement-learning tasks.

title: Skill issue: Lessons from skilling up coding agents to use Langfuse - Marc Klingen, Clickhouse
summary: Marc Klingen explains how Langfuse used execution traces and lightweight evaluations to improve a coding-agent integration skill. Traces exposed stale SDK assumptions, hallucinated CLI flags, and instrumentation that captured model calls but missed retrieval and tool activity. Five example setups supplied natural-language checks, judged against filesystem changes, to detect regressions. An automated skill-improvement experiment produced six proposals, three accepted, but minimizing turns encouraged removing documentation retrieval and other important workflow steps. Missing approval interactions and prompt-version links illustrated gaps in the objective and sandbox. The Q&A emphasizes human review and application-specific guidance rather than treating automated optimization as a complete substitute for expert judgment.

title: Benchmarking semantic code retrieval on Claude Code — Kuba Rogut, Turbopuffer
summary: Kuba Rogut evaluates semantic code retrieval using ContextBench-style human labels for files, lines and symbols an agent should inspect, rather than only task completion. Fifty tasks compare baseline Claude Code, fifty-line windowed reads and those reads plus a Voyage/turbopuffer search tool. Semantic search improves precision, but recall varies: behaviorally related files benefit, while import tracing often favors grep. The talk distinguishes adding an external tool from training a harness to use retrieval well, helping explain differences from Cursor’s results. It also frames embeddings as cached computation whose value depends on repeated workload and indexing cost.

title: SWE-rebench: Lessons from Evaluating Coding Agents — Ibragim Badertdinov, Nebius
summary: Ibragim Badertdinov explains SWE-rebench’s monthly collection of fresh software-engineering tasks to reduce contamination. Each task needs a balanced issue description, executable environment and verifier with both fail-to-pass and regression tests. Filtering, manual review and agent trials expose brittle tests and infrastructure noise. The talk details retry policies, caching, changing provider defaults and replicating known scores before new experiments. Reward-hacking examples include future Git history, web tools and curl recovering original solutions. Repeated trials support confidence intervals and distinguish pass-at-five potential from all-five reliability, while trajectory analysis supplies richer evidence than a mean resolution score.

title: Evals Are Broken, Use Them Anyway — Ara Khan, Cline
summary: Ara Khan rejects both treating leaderboard numbers as objective truth and abandoning evaluations for subjective preference. Cline’s experience building realistic tasks leads into Terminal-Bench and Harbor, where isolated standardized environments run long coding workflows in parallel. Failure traces are categorized to identify model limitations, harness bugs and infrastructure constraints such as memory, CPU and timeouts. The talk distinguishes obvious repairs, nuanced model-specific harness improvements and dangerous overfitting. Its recommendation is to use relevant, current benchmarks alongside real product experience, recognizing that the tested unit includes model, harness, task definition and execution environment rather than model weights alone.

title: SWE-Marathon: Evaluating Coding Agents at Billion-Token Scale - Rishi Desai, Abundant AI
summary: Rishi Desai presents SWE-Marathon, a twenty-task benchmark for project-scale coding work rather than isolated patches. Tasks span library clones, full-stack products, machine learning and algorithms, with long trajectories and large token budgets. Verification combines hidden tests, reference comparisons, browser-based user workflows and anti-cheating checks because an agent can exploit weak tests over hours of execution. The talk reports a best resolution rate of 26% and distinguishes suspicious shortcuts from actual verifier bypass attempts. A compiler submission secretly invoking GCC illustrates why functional parity alone is insufficient. Public trajectories support inspection of failures and harness effects.

title: Teaching Coding Agents to do Spreadsheets - Nuno Campos, Witan Labs
summary: Nuno Campos describes improving spreadsheet agents from roughly 50% to 92% on an internal financial-analysis benchmark. A persistent JavaScript REPL replaced many sequential tools, enabling more efficient exploration and nearly eliminating task timeouts. Crucially, reliable formula-calculation and rendering engines gave agents feedback analogous to compilers and tests; incomplete engines instead created misleading failures. Evaluation also evolved from LLM-only judging toward deterministic comparisons against golden spreadsheets, applying identical inputs and comparing resulting outputs. Campos stresses inspecting traces because apparent reasoning failures can originate in broken tools, prompts, or examples. The durable investment is trustworthy feedback infrastructure, even as model capabilities and preferred interfaces change.

title: Your coding agent doesn't always follow your rules — Talha Sheikh, Checkout.com
summary: Talha Sheikh describes replacing repeated manual correction of coding agents with explicit verification contracts. His Vector harness uses hooks and configurable checks to test outputs when an agent finishes, feeding failures back for another attempt. He distinguishes better instructions and greater model capability from demonstrated reliability, and generalizes the pattern beyond one product to language-agnostic checks at session endings, commits, multi-agent handoffs, and asynchronous work. Deterministically invoked verification may also call an LLM judge where appropriate. Sheikh suggests stronger harnesses could enable cheaper models, but presents this as an argument rather than a controlled benchmark. The main contribution is enforceable, reusable completion checks.

title: Recursive Model Improvement — Lee Robinson, Cursor, SpaceXAI
summary: Lee Robinson describes Cursor’s model-improvement flywheel connecting user reports, online A/B tests, private evaluations, difficult training environments, and new checkpoints. Public tests were vulnerable to Git-history and internet solution lookup, so Cursor also uses held-out internal engineering tasks reflecting real workflows and behavioral preferences. Robinson discusses retiring saturated evals, generating verifiable feature-reconstruction tasks, and providing localized textual feedback to improve credit assignment across long trajectories. Evaluation compute includes repeated checkpoint testing, reward generation, and developing fresh tasks, not just a launch leaderboard. The broader research-automation discussion explains how stronger models can help build and judge the next generation’s training and evaluation materials.

title: In the Land of AI Agents, the Verifiers Are King — Tariq Shaukat, Sonar
summary: Tariq Shaukat argues that agent capability gains do not remove the need to verify reliability, security, complexity, and maintainability. He contrasts benchmark task horizons at different success thresholds and describes Sonar’s coding evaluations, which assess more than functional correctness. His Guide, Verify, Solve framework supplies architectural context and constraints, combines algorithmic analysis with agentic assessment, and maintains code quality through ongoing remediation. Verification belongs inside the agent loop, the CI review loop, and the maintenance loop rather than as an afterthought. Vendor-presented customer results illustrate the argument, but the central recommendation is a deliberate, zero-trust, multilayered system for evaluating what agents actually produce.

title: DeepSWE: A Contamination-Resistant Coding Benchmark — James Shi, Datacurve
summary: James Shi presents DeepSWE, a benchmark of 113 original, long-horizon software-engineering tasks across five languages and a broad repository pool. He explains why public pull-request-derived tests can leak solutions, reward implementation-specific details, and inadequately distinguish strong models. DeepSWE instead commissions realistic tasks, checks observable behavior, separates verifier and agent runtimes, and removes exploitable Git history. Qualitative rollout analysis reveals missed multipart requirements, differences in requirement adherence, and how benchmark instructions can suppress self-testing. Shi also acknowledges limitations: harness effects deserve separate study, and refactoring and bug-localization tasks remain underrepresented. The talk treats benchmark integrity and failure analysis as essential complements to leaderboard scores.

title: Benchmarks: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly — Ali Khial, G2i
summary: Khial recounts investigating why coding benchmarks fail to resemble engineering work or inspire trust. He decomposes a benchmark into instructions, agents, verifiers, harnesses, and resulting trajectories, then examines unrealistic or leaky prompts, economically questionable tasks, and tests tied to unspecified implementation details. Citing another team's comparison, he reports that SWE-bench Pro tasks sometimes accepted incorrect implementations or rejected correct ones. He also describes increasingly capable agents exploiting exposed repository history or internet traces. His proposed framework combines human-authored instructions focused on behavior and constraints, holistic behavioral grading, production-relevant tasks, novel private holdouts, and reporting that explains model behavior instead of presenting only leaderboard winners.

title: fighting slop with slop — Vaibhav Gupta, Boundary
summary: Vaibhav Gupta describes Boundary's attempt to ship a reliable programming language without conventional code reviews or standardized AI tools. Small architecture documents, genuinely read design proposals, and dependency checks establish durable constraints. Agents continuously generate BAML programs; other agents inspect their execution transcripts for incorrect behavior and unnecessary tool calls, with humans triaging proposed issues. Language features and skills can then be A/B tested for errors, tool use, and successful outcomes. Gupta also demonstrates architectural visualization, navigable execution traces, source-aware inspection, callable functions, inferred error types, and cross-language interoperability. His argument is that stronger tooling and enforceable invariants can replace exhaustive line-by-line reading, not that correctness becomes unnecessary.

title: Benchmarking Coding Agents on New vs Legacy Codebases — Denys Linkov, Wisedocs
summary: Linkov examines Wisedocs' decision to rebuild a complex medical-document pipeline from multiple legacy repositories into a monorepo. He revisits earlier refactoring tasks with newer coding models and harnesses, reporting less manual intervention and better tool use, while distinguishing execution cost from engineering effort. He cautions against interpreting advertised task horizons at modest success rates as dependable autonomy. A separate attempt to refactor the whole system quickly produced scaffolding rather than functioning model deployments, illustrating why completion claims need inspection. The broader case study weighs technical debt, business outcomes, developer participation, and timing; its discussion emphasizes explicit requirements, proof-of-concept validation, end-to-end verification, and human reviews that preserve shared understanding.

title: Guide, Verify, Solve — Anirban Chatterjee, Sonar
summary: Chatterjee frames AI coding's bottleneck as verification debt: faster generation can leave persistent complexity, security, and maintainability problems. He describes Sonar's model leaderboard as evaluating coding tasks across several quality dimensions rather than correctness alone, and argues that human review also suffers from overreliance on confident AI output. His proposed guide-verify-solve cycle supplies architectural constraints and relevant context, checks generated code independently, and lets agents remediate findings. The presentation demonstrates Sonar Vortex integration and extends verification from the inner coding loop to outer pull-request and CI/CD gates. Its central recommendation is bounded autonomy backed by repeatable, auditable, multilayer checks combining computational analysis and LLM review.

title: How to Kill the Code Review — Ankit Jain, Aviator
summary: Ankit Jain argues that AI-generated code makes line-by-line review a bottleneck, but eliminating review must not eliminate team alignment, mentorship, or architectural discussion. His proposed replacement captures decisions from coding sessions as acceptance criteria and combines them with an 'AI slop registry' of recurring review failures to generate test plans. Verification runs the application in previews and gathers behavioral evidence, including screenshots and database snapshots. Humans review intent, architecture, test coverage, and execution evidence rather than merely trusting another model's comments. He favors deterministic checks where possible and LLM assistance where necessary, emphasizing that tests derived only from generated code can repeat the implementation's blind spots.

title: The Last Human Code Review: Building Trust in AI-Generated Code — Itamar Friedman, Qodo
summary: Itamar Friedman treats code review as both quality verification and a mechanism for alignment and learning, then asks what infrastructure could gradually automate it. He argues that stronger models alone are insufficient: reviewers need codified team standards, architectural context, service contracts, past incidents, and developer discussions. A context engine should expose this knowledge in forms useful to both humans and agents, linking findings to the rules and evidence behind them. He proposes software graphs that reveal cross-repository dependencies and conflicting changes, plus analytics showing which rules actually help. Automatic approval and blocking should expand incrementally through explicit semantic policies, rather than immediately removing human oversight.

title: Can LLMs Write Fast Multi-GPU Kernels? — Simran Arora, Together AI
summary: Simran Arora introduces ParallelKernelBench to test whether frontier models can generate useful multi-GPU CUDA kernels, after explaining communication bottlenecks and the ParallelKittens primitives. The benchmark contains 87 real-workload problems, each supplying a PyTorch reference and hardware topology. Evaluation separates functional correctness from kernels that also outperform the baseline, including pass-at-K and speedup-threshold comparisons. More sampling and a multi-turn bash-enabled agent improve results but plateau; compiling successfully does not imply understanding collective ordering, partitioning or communication tradeoffs. Reported zero-shot best-model performance is 28 correct kernels, 22 faster than baseline. The talk emphasizes realistic task coverage and analyzing which familiar patterns models solve.

title: Building the Engine While Flying the Plane: Launching the Figma MCP Server — Jesse Lumarie, Figma
summary: Jesse Lumarie recounts building Figma’s MCP server and the evaluation loop used to choose representations of design context. The team combined measurable checks, such as variable and theme usage, with qualitative judgments about visual quality and decisions under incomplete information. Manual spreadsheet grading proved too cumbersome, so they built an evaluation web app and assembled toy repositories with paired design files. The resulting workflow runs hundreds of times weekly and uses LLM judges to assess prompt changes. The talk also distinguishes pixel-perfect output from enterprise usefulness: generated implementations should reuse accessible, internationalized code components rather than merely resemble the design.

title: Building uReview, Uber’s Multi-Agent Code Review Engine — Will Bond & Ameya Ketkar, Uber
summary: Will Bond and Ameya Ketkar explain how Uber improved uReview by moving beyond cost tracking and broad satisfaction surveys. They collect review-reply sentiment, whether developers address comments, and agent trajectories to identify weak rules, wasted actions and runtime issues. Distributed team-specific reviewers share central routing, filtering and deduplication, with observability returned to rule owners. Reported production scale is about 25,000 comments weekly, with roughly 67% addressed and a 60% cost reduction versus their naive implementation. They distinguish human-facing from agent-inner-loop reviews, where inaccurate comments can cause repeated reversals. Their conclusion preserves a human outer feedback loop focused on architecture, domain expertise and product judgment.

title: Your Code Has Bugs. Lean4 Has Proofs: Formal Verification for Engineers — Varun Pant, AWS
summary: Varun Pant introduces formal verification as a complement to probabilistic judges, sampled tests and limited human review for AI-generated code. The key contract is an explicit specification: humans must validate what correctness means before machines implement it and construct proofs. He explains Lean’s tactics and independently checkable trusted kernel, then discusses a reported zlib conversion and Cedar’s Lean specification paired with Rust production code. Cedar’s differential random testing is distinguished from direct deductive proof. Further examples include Verus preconditions and postconditions and AWS’s work-in-progress Strata framework. The practical message is to start with critical code and verified specifications, not assume proofs establish unstated requirements.

title: Fixing the PR Bottleneck — Matt Pocock, AIHero
summary: Matt Pocock proposes three quality brakes for agent-driven software factories: deterministic checks, automated review and human review. He illustrates why green CI can mislead through tautological assertions, source-structure tests and mocks that erase real failure modes. Deep modules with narrow interfaces make behavior-focused tests easier. A separate reviewer context applies repository-specific standards and, in his proposed workflow, commits fixes before humans see the change. Human attention is allocated by reversibility and blast radius rather than diff size alone. Finally, retrospectives convert recurring review findings into stronger checks, standards and navigation guidance, improving the system that produces code rather than repeatedly correcting identical mistakes.

title: AI-Generated Code Is Already Competing With Human Code — Daksh Gupta, Greptile
summary: Gupta examines whether largely autonomous coding agents produce enterprise-worthy pull requests using Greptile's review data. He infers AI authorship from author fields, description footers, and branch prefixes, reporting about a quarter of reviewed PRs as largely AI-generated. Revert rates, detected high-severity bugs, and review iterations show broadly comparable human and agent outcomes in his analysis, while keyword-based error categories reveal differing failure profiles. These are observational proxies with imperfect authorship labels and reviewer-dependent quality signals, not proof of equivalent capability on matched tasks. He argues validation must scale with PR generation, assessing user-contract violations, future risk, and author intent through contextual review and sandbox execution.

title: The Death of the Code Review: What the Data Actually Says — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
summary: Voss examines why rapid AI code generation has not translated proportionally into shipped software, framing human review as a bottleneck. He contrasts test-passing benchmarks with maintainer mergeability, surveys multipass and tool-using automated reviewers, and revisits autonomous coding experiments whose human judgment moved into harnesses rather than disappearing. Claimed case studies highlight maintenance problems, unsafe-code blind spots, and prompt-injection vulnerabilities in reviewers. His conclusion is not to abandon verification but to encode domain context, quality standards, and review criteria into an engineered system. Humans still assess that system, especially where consequences are large or correctness is expensive to check, while production observability provides essential downstream evidence.

title: Agentic Search vs Vector Search for Coding Agents: We Ran the Eval — Braintrust
summary: Jess introduces evaluations as datasets, executable tasks, scoring systems, and comparative experiments that support evidence-based shipping decisions. Her example compares vector retrieval with tool-driven agentic search on roughly 20 bug-fix tasks reconstructed from Microsoft's TypeScript-Go repository. Both approaches use Claude Code, with tool restrictions enforcing the vector condition; subprocess trace linkage makes behavior inspectable, and repository tests provide binary scoring. She reports equal accuracy but fourfold higher cost for vector search, attributing repeated retrieval to chunks lacking cross-function context. She explicitly limits the finding: the vector implementation was weak, the dataset small and single-repository, and repeated trials and broader coverage would strengthen confidence. The purpose is methodological illustration, not a definitive retrieval ranking.

title: We Mapped 115 Microservices for Our Coding Agents — Kamalakannan Nandagopal, Postman
summary: Kamalakannan Nandagopal describes evaluating Postman’s API context graph using real pull requests and retrospective design decisions as task ground truth. The team compares its agent, Claude Code using GitHub search, and Claude Code with graph access through a skill, scoring outputs from zero to five and measuring token consumption. Examples cover API discovery, input-shape reconstruction, and change-impact assessment. He reports quality and efficiency benefits in selected cases, but also an inverted result when newly added consumers were missing from the graph. The presentation therefore highlights freshness as an evaluation dependency; it does not supply a complete dataset or statistical validation of general superiority.

title: How to Build an AI Code Review Agent - Daksh Gupta, Greptile
summary: Daksh Gupta outlines how to build an effective code-review agent beyond a basic webhook and sandbox. The difficult requirements are finding substantive bugs, suppressing nitpicks, understanding a large codebase, and keeping review costs manageable. He recommends a continuously updated evaluation set of historical incident-causing pull requests, focused prompts, contextual documentation, and autonomous end-to-end tests. Greptile reportedly detects about 10% more bugs when a different model family reviews the generating model’s code. He also discusses routing inexpensive models to simpler subtasks. His caution is fundamental: finding bugs demonstrates their presence, but a clean review cannot prove their absence, so validation must keep evolving as agents produce new failure modes.

title: Building Closed-Loop Evals for a Multimodal Agent at Scale — Soumya Gupta & Jai Chopra, Uber
summary: Soumya Gupta and Jai Chopra describe Uber Eats’ evaluation system for enhancing merchant food photographs without changing the dish, erasing branding, or homogenizing the marketplace. Human-labeled, representative examples anchor routing precision and recall, while editing agents receive multidimensional QA feedback and bounded regeneration attempts. Pairwise input/output checks assess faithfulness, completeness, naturalness, and realism; uncertain cases can be rejected. Production samples, merchant feedback, and marketplace metrics feed a diagnoser that routes failures to configuration and prompt-tuning loops. Updated agents must clear the golden benchmark before registration. The talk highlights reward hacking, redundant final publication checks, observability, segment-level analysis, and rollback as safeguards around automated improvement.

title: How Kepler Built Verifiable AI for Financial Services — Vinoo Ganesh
summary: Vinoo Ganesh argues that citations and probabilistic evaluations cannot by themselves guarantee numerically reliable financial work. He describes Kepler's three-part architecture: atomic provenance, scoped determinism, and derivation chains. Models select references and decide what should be computed, while deterministic systems extract, persist, validate, and calculate numbers. Unverifiable values are removed rather than passed through. Derivation chains record source data and transformations so ratios and adjustments can be replayed under a firm's particular conventions. Ganesh distinguishes verifying a process from proving an investment opinion correct, since identical evidence can support opposing positions. The discussion extends the approach to legal and scientific entities and ends with customers' interest in automating repetitive analyst tasks.

title: Build for the Memo, Not the Demo — Shawn Chan, China Resources Holdings
summary: Shawn Chan evaluates finance AI from the perspective of an investment-committee decision maker rather than a builder. A polished demo is insufficient when a memo must survive scrutiny across conflicting filings, notes, transcripts, and spreadsheets. He identifies six trust failures: unreliable source selection, inconsistent numbers, concealed contradictions, guesses presented as facts, inaccessible evidence, and missing accountability. His proposed controls link each claim to an exact source passage and trust level, visibly separate assumptions, automatically reconcile figures, surface disagreements, and log human approval. The closing fundraising lesson applies the same standard to founders: pitch claims eventually become internal investment memos whose numbers are checked against the data room.

title: "My name is... my name is...": A Linguistic Map for Voice Agents — Midam Kim, ServiceNow
summary: Midam Kim analyzes a failed voice-agent call through a linguistic framework rather than treating each defect as an isolated bug. Misheard spelling, English-centric pronunciation, premature turn-taking, unfamiliar account terminology and repeated requests accumulate into user frustration. Her framework crosses listening and speaking with sounds, words, interaction and mental models. These layers are interdependent and evolve over a call, so strong speech recognition alone cannot guarantee task success. She recommends using this structure to diagnose an agent and references ServiceNow’s EVA end-to-end benchmark. The central evaluation contribution is a systematic error taxonomy connected to escalation, abandonment, silent failures and the user’s evolving understanding.

title: 5 Voice Agent Failure Modes You'll Hit in Week One — Venky B, Plivo
summary: Venky B organizes production voice failures into latency, brittle transcription, data collection, speech normalization and turn-taking problems. He discusses measuring time to first audio and balancing model capability, cost and response speed, including multilingual tokenization effects. The most concrete evaluation recommendation is to model collected information as typed fields with validators and confirmations, then test each field independently instead of running expensive end-to-end conversations to discover a broken input. He reports substantial data-collection improvements without fine-tuning through this structural approach. Proper nouns, code-switching, relative dates and pronunciation are practical stress cases. The talk emphasizes engineering reliable subcomponents rather than repeatedly tweaking prompts and hoping compliance improves.

title: The Transcript Looked Fine. The Call Wasn't. — Debugging Voice Agents, Arize
summary: This Arize talk argues that transcripts alone conceal important voice-agent failures: pauses, overlapping speech, transcription errors, tone, and incorrect downstream actions. An AI-generated refund example illustrates a misheard order number, dead air, and a refund issued for the wrong order despite superficially reassuring text. The presenter advocates linking audio, transcripts, tool spans, and multi-turn sessions through normalized OpenInference conventions. Audio-aware evaluations should measure time to first audio, interruptions, sentiment, transcription drift, and actual task success, with results attached to relevant spans. The closing vision extends observation into agent-led diagnosis, replay-based fix validation, and reviewable pull requests; this self-healing workflow is presented as a future direction rather than proven end-to-end performance.

title: Don't Trust Your AI Agents. Test Them Like a Scientist — Stephanie Jarmak, Omni Analytics
summary: Stephanie Jarmak argues that agent evaluation should resemble a controlled experiment. She shows that changing the harness alone can move benchmark performance by more than thirty percentage points, so a score cannot be attributed to the model without accounting for configuration. Public benchmarks help shortlist candidates; product decisions require realistic local tasks, repeated runs, appropriate measures, and full-pipeline traces. She discusses balancing retrieval precision and recall, enforcing quality gates that actually stop work, and budgeting the human workload created by alarms. Agent-maintained records may be unreliable evidence. Production feedback ultimately tests whether offline improvements survive real conditions, and escalation should be designed around risk rather than a single aggregate success rate.

title: Can AI Understand a Distressed Credit? - Harneet Kaur, Axim Intelligence
summary: Harneet Kaur asks how to assess AI reasoning when the final outcome has not happened yet. In a live distressed-credit case involving iHeartMedia, frontier models given similar context initially assign sharply different bankruptcy probabilities. She decomposes the work into extraction, derivation, judgment, and prediction so that factual inputs and assumptions can be checked separately. Structured context and layer-by-layer evaluation bring the models toward a common answer, but she explicitly questions whether convergence proves correctness. Historical testing also risks look-ahead bias. The talk’s contribution is a framework for exposing intermediate reasoning failures and assumptions, not evidence that consensus can validate an uncertain investment forecast.

title: The Multi-Agent Architecture That Actually Ships — Luke Alvoeiro, Factory
summary: Luke Alvoeiro presents Factory's Missions architecture, emphasizing verification as the mechanism that sustains long-running coding agents. An orchestrator defines features, milestones, and a validation contract before implementation. Workers execute tasks with clean contexts and provide structured handoffs containing commands, exit codes, and unresolved issues. Separate validators run conventional checks and feature reviews, then exercise the live application through user-like interactions. Failures generate corrective work at milestone boundaries. The talk favors serial feature execution with parallel read-only operations and assigns models by role. A Slack-clone example illustrates repeated validation failures and follow-up work, rather than treating passing unit tests as sufficient evidence of completion.

title: Anthropic Workshop: Build Agents That Run for Hours — Ash Prabaker & Andrew Wilson
summary: Prabaker and Wilson examine long-running agents through context management, planning, and unreliable self-assessment. Their central pattern separates a generator from an adversarial evaluator that exercises live applications with browser tools rather than merely reviewing code. Subjective design quality becomes an explicit, example-calibrated rubric, while generator and evaluator negotiate testable contracts before implementation. A game-building comparison illustrates how interactive verification exposes broken behavior that superficial completeness and unit tests miss. Trace reading identifies where model judgment diverges from human expectations and guides prompt revisions. Q&A clarifies that evaluators should judge outputs without inheriting generator reasoning, and that rubric scores are useful within runs but not readily comparable across products.

title: Spec-Driven Testing for Agents With A Brain the Size of A Planet — Steven Willmott, SafeIntelligence
summary: Steven Willmott argues that an agent specification must contain more than input/output examples. It should explicitly state rules, domain ontologies, terminology, rights, roles and robustness requirements, independently of implementation. Larger models can understand more malicious instructions and broader tool access creates additional attack surface, so capability is not equivalent to safety. The same specification can guide security testing and valid input variations such as typos or rephrasings. Tests should survive framework or model changes and feed iterative repairs. The talk stresses that generating meaningful variants requires knowing which substitutions preserve domain meaning and permissions.

title: Agents Building Agents - Alfonso Graziano, Nearform
summary: Alfonso Graziano separates a coding agent that builds software from the product agent being evaluated. A golden dataset and scorers establish the baseline; an optimization loop proposes one hypothesis, edits prompts, tools or code, reruns evaluations and retains or rolls back changes. Reports and memory preserve unsuccessful experiments as well as gains. A second workflow collects production traces with user or expert feedback, clusters failure modes, validates them with domain experts and adds confirmed cases to regression coverage. The talk warns against letting the optimizing agent change datasets or scorers simply to make scores improve.

title: Frontier results, on device - RL Nabors, Arize
summary: RL Nabors demonstrates selecting small local models through application-specific capability evaluations rather than public reputation. A thread-summarization case uses a golden dataset, deterministic checks for JSON, references and length, plus an LLM judge for factual consistency and latency measurements. The process prototypes with a capable remote model, tests smaller alternatives, and isolates prompt changes one variable at a time. Inspecting individual failures exposes overly strict judging and format problems better handled by post-processing. The resulting model and prompt are retained as regression tests so future migrations cannot silently undo quality or responsiveness gains.

title: The Agentic AI Engineer - Benedikt Sanftl, Mutagent
summary: Benedikt Sanftl and Burak describe automating the offline and online loops of agent engineering. Specifications establish responsibilities and success criteria; evaluation datasets and metrics evolve from real failures rather than appearing complete at the start. Evaluators inspect context completeness, tool outputs, trajectories and harness effects, favoring actionable binary criteria and calibrated judges over ambiguous scores. Production diagnosis groups failures by root cause and derives new tests before optimization. The demo produces trace-linked explanations, assumptions and candidate remedies for human decisions, while sampling and learned indicators reduce the cost of repeatedly reading large trace collections.

title: What Does Done Even Mean? Agents and Paperclip's Liveness Model - Dotta, Paperclip
summary: Dotta argues that “done” must represent a bundle of operational claims rather than an agent-controlled Boolean. An artifact may exist without being reviewed, independently verified, authorized for release, or proven under real-world conditions. Paperclip’s liveness model balances productive progress against verification through explicit transitions, blockers, reviewers, approvers, watchdogs, and bounded loops. The proposed completion record includes scope, rubric, evidence, verifier, approval authority, residual risk, and next action. Dotta recommends separating author and verifier, often across models, and giving agents practical tools such as browsers and screenshots to demonstrate completion. The central goal is replacing approval theater with inspectable evidence and clear custody.

title: Your Agents Need a Save Button - Hamza Tahir, ZenML
summary: Hamza Tahir distinguishes read-only traces from durable execution checkpoints that preserve code, artifacts, environment, and intermediate state. With checkpoints, teams can replay a production run from a chosen decision, change a model or tool result, and compare outcomes against the original. A Kitaru demonstration extends individual replays into cohort-level analysis of support cases, showing why a cheaper model that looks acceptable once may fail across a meaningful distribution. Tahir warns against optimizing token cost without task value or shipping after one or two examples. His proposed loop is checkpoint, replay, diff, and decide, using representative production cohorts and retaining human approval.

title: Perception Agents — Antje Barth, Amazon AGI Lab
summary: Antje Barth argues that computer-use capability is insufficient without observing whether actions actually achieved the intended result. She introduces open-source perception-agent components for shared visual annotation and verification against design specifications. The verification demonstration checks rendered appearance, brand and layout rules, and actual application flows such as adding or deleting tasks, then produces a pass/fail report for human review. Shared screen context and precise annotations reduce ambiguous instructions, while a meeting-transcript example feeds requested changes directly into implementation and verification. The talk is a product-pattern demonstration rather than a calibrated benchmark, but its central concern is closing the observe-act-check loop for reliable agent work.

title: Persona Engineering: A Field Guide to AI Synthetic Personas — Ishan Anand, InsightSciences.ai
summary: Ishan Anand frames synthetic personas as bounded forecasts, not replacements for people. He reviews research on interview-grounded personas, prompting, fine-tuning, and mapping free-text responses onto survey distributions. Failure modes include invented contextual confounders, strong option-order sensitivity, amplified demographic bias, and weaker prediction of behavior than stated attitudes. Evaluation must compare synthetic responses with human ground truth using both correlation and distribution-shape metrics. Repeated synthetic sampling does not create additional statistical significance. Anand recommends estimating human inconsistency through retesting or repeated data splits; he cites a study's 83% alignment as normalized against human noise. Synthetic personas can extend existing research, but require empirical calibration and continuing reality checks.

title: Memory Harnesses for Long-Running Research Agents — Stefania Druga, Sakana.ai
summary: Stefania Druga evaluates local research-agent memory as a write-manage-read control loop, holding the model fixed while varying recall policies. Conditions include no memory, vector retrieval, a ranked decision ledger, and an oracle supplying the correct memory. A literature-review task already fitting in context gains no capability from added memory, only cost. For longer-horizon XBench tasks, she reports that ranked ledger recall performs best across tested conditions, with additional ablations and SpiderV2 experiments. Importantly, oracle retrieval does not guarantee correct answers because a model may ignore or misuse supplied evidence. She argues for evaluating recall policy and token cost explicitly, while noting local hardware and serial-inference constraints.

title: Context Engineering in 2026 — Louis-François Bouchard, Omar Solano & Samridhi Vaid, Towards AI
summary: The Towards AI team evaluates context-management strategies for its tutoring agent using real student questions, synthetic multi-turn recall probes, deterministic retrieval checks, and LLM grading. They compare fixed configurations while logging cost, latency, caching, and whether compaction actually triggered. Contrary to their initial defaults, retaining history often beats summarization or clearing tool outputs, which can destroy cache reuse and force retrieval again. The speakers report roughly 95% detail recall with full history versus 32% after summarization, while acknowledging limited trials in the initial experiments. Local context limits change the trade-off: hybrid retrieval helps oversized documents, but chat memory remains weaker. Their selected setup uses cached DeepSeek V4 Flash, hybrid retrieval, and a compaction threshold.

title: Don’t be data poor — Anuj Iravane, Anterior
summary: Anuj Iravane describes building healthcare evaluation datasets when contracts prohibit retaining patient records or derivative copies. Anterior reverses its policy-guided inference task: sample an outcome and a symbolic policy reasoning trace, then generate supporting records. A coarse-to-fine pipeline creates patient invariants, journeys, encounter plans, and documents, followed by consistency checks and round-trip validation against the intended label. Clinicians can steer generation and own pipeline logic through skills, allowing realistic failure cases without engineering changes. Iravane says synthetic data is currently used for evaluation, not training, and constitutes roughly 90% of their datasets. He reports clinicians distinguished synthetic from real records about 60% of the time in blind review.

title: Act, Confirm, or Stop? Smarter behavior for AI assistants, wearables & robots — Amit Desai, Roku
summary: Amit Desai demonstrates how to improve voice-assistant outcomes without improving recognition accuracy. In a simplified music-request example, he assigns different user recovery costs to wrong actions, refusals and confirmations, then optimizes confidence thresholds against their combined cost. This Outcome User Cost Heuristic, or OUCH, exposes why an intuitive threshold can be inferior to a data-driven one. Adding a confirmation region changes the decision policy while leaving the underlying model unchanged. He extends the reasoning to televisions and embodied assistants, where interface modality and action consequences alter the cost model. The talk advocates evaluating user harm and recovery effort rather than accuracy in isolation.

title: The unreasonable effectiveness of BM25 for agentic search — Jo Kristian Bergum, Hornet.dev
summary: Jo Kristian Bergum argues that search evaluation must change when the searcher is an agent capable of reformulating many queries. Using BrowseComp-Plus, he contrasts high accuracy when evidence is supplied directly with lower end-to-end accuracy through a search tool, isolating retrieval and harness limitations from reasoning. He warns that an inadequately configured BM25 baseline can make competing methods appear stronger than they are; parameter and implementation choices matter. Rather than judge a single ranked list alone, he recommends measuring whether the complete agent reaches the correct answer. The talk also discusses query trajectories and filesystem workspaces as practical retrieval interfaces.

title: The Loop Is the Product — Roland Gavrilescu, Introspection
summary: Roland Gavrilescu argues that agent products improve through nested loops: workers generate traces and outcomes, while a second loop turns recurring failures into judges, evaluations, skills and harness changes. He proposes portable, versioned agent recipes that preserve this accumulated judgment independently of a model provider. A recruiting example shows how trace analysis reveals undesirable targeting, humans calibrate a judge, and agents generate candidate changes. Offline evaluations are necessary but insufficient: production experiments must establish that users value the creator’s preferences before a recipe is promoted. His proposed optimization target is valuable work relative to its resource cost, not raw token consumption.

title: The Self-Improving OSS Agent Stack — Marc Klingen, Langfuse
summary: Klingen outlines an emerging open-source stack linking production traces, feedback, evaluation datasets, and automated improvement experiments. Agents can increasingly propose implementation fixes and maintain evaluation assets, but humans should approve changes that redefine optimization targets to avoid irrelevant failure chasing and overfitting. A changelog-writing demo uses human approval and edit signals to identify internal jargon and unclear customer language. Updated datasets compare a baseline and candidate, showing improved user-facing language without degrading format or accuracy in the example. Automatic release is acceptable there because the writer only opens reviewable pull requests. He also emphasizes scalable, retained trace data as agent-driven analysis becomes increasingly read-intensive.

title: Parameter Golf with AutoResearch — Vayum Arora, Zhengyao Jiang, Dixing Xu & Dhruv Srikanth, Weco AI
summary: Weco AI demonstrates autoresearch as a loop that proposes code changes, evaluates them, keeps improvements, and discards worse attempts. Mini Parameter Golf supplies a small training task, a fixed command, and a scalar validation objective; a dashboard records code and scores in an experiment tree. The presenters emphasize fast, stable measurements, correct optimization direction, bounded runtime, useful initial guidance, and protecting the evaluator from reward hacking. A second exercise optimizes a Flappy Bird controller across several conditions, with a hidden validation set and restricted editable code. Human steering can explore promising branches, but meaningful progress depends on the quality and integrity of the evaluation signal.

title: The Data Context Layer for Agents — Yoni Michael & Brandon Callender, Typedef
summary: Yoni Michael and Brandon Callender combine data-context architecture with a substantial evaluation workshop. Their comparisons hold model and task fixed while varying graph versus filesystem tools, using repeated runs, source-checked gold answers, deterministic citation checks, token counts, and tool-adoption traces. Callender distinguishes occasional success from correctness across every run, reporting stronger consistency and lower token use for the graph approach in a cached experiment. He also describes misleading early results caused by broken file paths, and repository-history leakage in bug-fixing evaluations. The presenters recommend hardening scorers and harnesses, reading traces, and pinning corpus snapshots; reported gains remain specific to their tasks and setup.

title: 1,000 Agent Tasks in a Sandbox: What Breaks When LLMs Run Code — Kevin Orellana, AWS
summary: Kevin Orellana uses coding agents to test the infrastructure those agents themselves depend on. An MCP wrapper exposes AgentCore’s code sandbox and browser, and agents generate and execute one thousand workflows across ten domains, logging results in SQLite for concurrent analysis. Failures include incorrect image encoding, null-byte handling, unreadable files, and browser memory exhaustion. He separates interface-layer defects from sandbox limits involving permissions, memory, process creation, seccomp, and eBPF. The talk also considers the limitations of model-generated tests and benchmark exploits. His recommendation is broad remote workflow fuzzing alongside local tests, because infrastructure failures can masquerade as weak agent reasoning or prevent an otherwise capable agent from completing its task.

title: Containment Is Lying to You: Measuring AI Agents Like Employees — Druid AI
summary: Druid AI critiques containment rate as a misleading proxy for agent success. An agent escalating fewer conversations may look better while missing customers who actually need human attention. The presenters propose a seven-pillar scorecard covering configuration, runtime behavior, and governance, with twenty-six components scored by whether they are absent, defined, or actively governed. Business-weighted checks include mandate, permissions, budget, risk, compliance, observability, hallucination, tone, and validated outcomes. Repeated measurement against a human baseline can expose degradation hidden behind an unchanged green dashboard. The framework emphasizes matching metrics to a specific business role and industry; its composite score is a proposed management instrument, not an independently established universal benchmark.

title: Just-in-Time Ontologies: What Cheap Intelligence Means for Data — Hrishi Olickel, Southbridge AI
summary: Hrishi Olickel presents just-in-time ontologies as transformations built around a specific decision rather than a universal schema. The evaluation lessons come from data-work examples: ambiguous entity definitions, costly checking, and a pipeline that removed negative signs and turned a much smaller net balance into millions of debt while multiple models agreed. He separates designers, task workers, and optimizers, and recommends held-out cases, bounded pilot runs, versioned work segments, and explicit failure conditions. Cross-model disagreement can concentrate human review, but consensus can preserve shared mistaken assumptions. Cost, speed, and accuracy optimization only becomes meaningful when the execution surface, baseline, and evidence are stable enough to compare.

title: How to Know If Your AI Agent Is Any Good: Evals With Phoenix & Claude — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
summary: Laurie Voss builds an evaluation loop around a Claude-powered financial analyst, beginning with Phoenix tracing and manual error analysis. A report claiming 116% analyst agreement illustrates why plausible final prose is insufficient. Code checks cover deterministic properties; model judges assess faithfulness and actionability. A generic correctness judge fails partly because it lacks fresh evidence, so she supplies research context and creates a focused custom judge. Human labels, rubric disagreements, and development/test separation help calibrate it. Repeated prompt experiments improve actionability without fixing all faithfulness failures, and a model upgrade introduces conservatism. The workshop ends with CI acceptance criteria and ongoing production sampling, emphasizing complementary measures rather than one score.

title: Evals for High-Stakes AI Agents — Doneyli De Jesus & Annabell Schäfer, Langfuse
summary: Annabell Schäfer and Doneyli De Jesus walk through a Langfuse evaluation loop for a fictional banking assistant. Tracing captures intermediate work, with PII masking before persistence; production samples and imported cases become datasets. Domain experts annotate outputs, comments are grouped into failure modes, and focused code checks or LLM judges score experiments. The session demonstrates prompt-change evaluation in CI and dashboards linking quality findings to operational concerns. Judge calibration against representative human labels is essential, particularly in regulated applications. A demonstrated score gate illustrates the intended workflow, but its effectiveness depends on testing candidates before promotion and connecting the gate correctly to deployment rather than merely displaying pass/fail results.

title: Teach Your Agent to Prove It's Done — Nick Nisi & Zack Proser, WorkOS
summary: Nick Nisi and Zack Proser demonstrate how coding agents can produce checkable evidence instead of merely announce that a task is finished. The Midnight Snack Club application combines explicit goals, CLI health checks, browser observations, deterministic tests, and model judges. Failures feed the next repair attempt, while independent evidence includes screenshots, smoke tests, and persisted application state. The live discussion exposes limitations: a judge may miss a successful interaction, and a saved receipt may refer to code that has since changed. They advocate a stable evaluation baseline that multiple implementations can target, with checks tied to the current artifact and real user journeys rather than a passing build alone.

title: What Agents Want — Dan Barrett, Raymond Weitekamp & Jose Montes de Oca, OpenProse
summary: The OpenProse team proposes expressing multi-agent work as declarative contracts in Markdown rather than prescribing every implementation step. Demos include event-triggered jobs, a deliberately critical PR reviewer, and bank model documentation. Evaluation is embedded in the contract: describe the desired end state, compare runs against that specification, and preserve successful trajectories as reusable workflows. The presenters discuss development versus production behavior, historical-result comparisons, composable contracts, and differences from DSPy. The approach shifts effort toward stating what success means, but it does not remove the need for a trustworthy checker or good examples. The session presents workflow mechanics rather than independently measured reliability gains.

title: Backtest Your Agent Against Yesterday's Web — Ryan Ahern, Exa
summary: Ryan Ahern leads a workshop using historical search to backtest agent-generated predictions.
