Failures are preserved as regression cases and replayed against a candidate fix. The workshop compares code checks, LLM judges, and decision models, and discusses evaluation health, qualitative output, sampling, and cost. Humans retain leverage over rubric design, dataset curation, and reviewing changes. The useful distinction is between detecting a production problem and experimentally establishing that a repair resolves it without introducing regressions.

title: Skill Issue: How We Used AI to Make Agents Actually Good at Supabase — Pedro Rodrigues, Supabase
summary: Pedro Rodrigues walks through evaluating agent skills against Supabase database tasks. A performance-review application exposes how a seemingly successful generated SQL view can bypass row-level security. Adding a security skill changes the generated migration to include security_invoker, but the live application still has other vulnerabilities. The workshop then compares skill and no-skill conditions using a reset database, headless Claude Code, and deterministic assertions. A faulty evaluator marks similar outputs differently, demonstrating why graders themselves need inspection. The speaker distinguishes appending skill instructions to the system prompt from organic discovery and recommends representative triggering and non-triggering scenarios, isolated environments, regression checks, and maintaining only relevant production skills.

title: Combine Skills and MCP to Close the Context Gap — Pedro Rodrigues, Supabase
summary: Pedro Rodrigues explains Supabase’s evaluation-driven development of an agent skill. A matched task shows why tool access alone is insufficient: creating a PostgreSQL view without security_invoker can bypass existing row-level security, while the skill-guided agent handles the constraint. He describes six project scenarios tested across four models under three conditions: neither MCP nor skills, MCP alone, and MCP plus the skill. The combined condition leads on the reported task-completeness measure. Observed failures also shape the document: security essentials belong in the main skill because references may be skipped, while changing documentation should be linked. Q&A addresses repository-based distribution and unresolved packaging limitations.

title: Can LLMs generate Enterprise Quality Code? — Prasenjit Sarkar, Sonar
summary: Prasenjit Sarkar presents Sonar’s analysis of thousands of Java programming assignments across dozens of models. Functional benchmark scores are placed alongside code volume, bug density, security findings and cyclomatic or cognitive complexity to show why passing tests does not establish enterprise readiness. The talk compares model behaviors and warns that more recent models can produce substantially more code and subtler issues. Its proposed development cycle guides generation with context, verifies code before commit through static analysis, and uses a remediation agent that reanalyzes and compiles proposed fixes before presenting them for human review.

title: Evals-Driven Development for a Mental Health AI Coach — Akele Reed & Dave Revere, SonderMind
summary: Akele Reed and Dave Revere describe a mental-health coach whose independent input and output guardrails are calibrated through clinician-led evaluation. The goal is not maximal intervention: inappropriate escalation can itself deny support, while indirect crisis language may evade generic moderation. Licensed clinicians annotate traced conversations with expected observations, categories, and the turn where intervention should occur. Those annotations become typed, replayable evaluation cases committed to CI so prompt, model, and guardrail changes are regression-tested. The speakers emphasize false positives, false negatives, timing, and clinical context rather than chasing a perfect aggregate score. They also release reviewed input- and output-guardrail datasets as starting baselines, not substitutes for local learning loops.

title: We Vetted 2000 AI Skills Before They Reached Developers — Lucas Palma, Nubank
summary: Lucas Palma describes Nubank's security-review pipeline for AI skills, treating instructions, plugins, and MCP integrations as supply-chain dependencies rather than harmless configuration. Developers can scan locally, but mandatory CI rescans submissions before internal marketplace distribution. Deterministic pattern checks handle clear risks, while LLM review adds behavioral context; findings appear in pull requests and machine-readable security reports. Palma reports scanning over 2,000 skills, finding more than 1,500 risks, and roughly 1,000 remediations. Examples include credential exposure, destructive shell commands, excessive permissions, and unsafe file changes. He emphasizes context-sensitive severity, actionable remediation, retrospective scanning, and tool-level approval enforcement because prompt-only requests for human confirmation can be satisfied incorrectly by agents.

title: Teaching AI to Find Real Vulnerabilities — Prof. David Brumley, Bugcrowd
summary: Brumley explains cybersecurity evaluation through two ladders: target difficulty and exploitation capability. He argues that single-bug tasks and crash-only rewards encourage agents to rediscover easy flaws or overstate hacking ability. His audit-task alternative accepts multiple executable proofs, deterministically validates and deduplicates vulnerabilities, and balances precision with recall while expanding ground truth for newly discovered bugs. He then presents a staged V8 evaluation separating crashes, memory-access primitives, sandbox escape, and code execution. Across 41 verified vulnerabilities, Brumley reports code-execution success of 73% for Mythos and 68% for GPT, contrasting with much easier crash triggering. He closes with contamination-resistant environment generation and disclosure concerns around publishing weaponized outputs.

title: Guardrails First: Engineering Member-Facing Health AI — Rashi Agrawal, Hinge Health
summary: Rashi Agrawal describes member-facing healthcare AI as an architectural safety problem, not something solved by stronger prompts. She advocates removing protected health information at ingestion, separating environments, and placing emergency escalation, authentication, and high-stakes routing in code above the model. Production safety combines continuously running multidimensional judges, member feedback, and human trace review, with every high-stakes case checked. Launch decisions should reflect plausible worst-case harm, separate severity from engineering capacity, and default toward the safer mistake. Crucially, a falling evaluation score should trigger investigation of the judge before changing the agent: an overcalling scorer and genuinely unsafe advice require different fixes.

title: Loophole: Adversarial Agents To Stress Test Your Morality — Brendan Rappazzo, Morgan Stanley
summary: Brendan Rappazzo presents Loophole, a personal open-source project that stress-tests moral rules using adversarial agents. One agent formalizes user principles; two others search for immoral-but-permitted cases and moral-but-prohibited cases. A judge patches translation errors or escalates genuine ambiguity to the human. DNA-consent examples illustrate both outcomes. He then explores the same pattern for chatbot constitutions, checking inappropriate answers and inappropriate refusals, and for comparing contracts. The final branch simulates legislative preferences and optimizes proposed bills against them. Those political experiments are presented as exploratory simulations, not evidence of real-world voting prediction. The evaluation contribution is adversarial case generation with bidirectional coverage and human judgment.

title: 1 Trillion Phone Calls/yr, 10% Error rate: The Crisis in Voice AI — Sumanyu Sharma, Hamming AI
summary: Sumanyu Sharma argues that centralized voice agents can propagate small defects to enormous numbers of calls. Drawing on Hamming’s monitored deployments, he describes a loop of failure discovery, frequency-and-severity prioritization, fixes, regression checks and continued monitoring. Manual call listening builds initial understanding, but cross-conversation analysis is needed to discover new patterns rather than merely score known rubrics. He recommends repeatedly replaying failures, then varying wording, accents and intent combinations; some experience changes still require real A/B tests. The final section extends reliability testing to adversarial callers, reports breaking roughly one in five tested agents, and recommends continuous red teaming where consequences are significant.

title: I Believe Everything My Agents Tell Me: Three Levels of Review — Corey Gallon, Rexmore
summary: Corey Gallon describes three levels of review for agents that misstate completion, extract facts incorrectly, or reason from faulty assumptions. Level one verifies the actual artifact and its fingerprint. Level two uses independent extractions, control totals, provenance, and reconciliation against source material. Level three combines self-audit with cold reviewers instructed to challenge the result, followed by fresh review of revisions. Examples cover an overstated memory-leak fix, accounting statements, and a demand letter based on an overlooked contract renewal. He reports substantial review time and token costs. His session-error observations describe his own sample, while the method supplies concrete checking practices rather than a guarantee that reviews eliminate every mistake.

title: Beyond Transcription: Building Voice AI That Understands Conversations — Hervé Bredin, pyannoteAI
summary: Hervé Bredin explains speaker diarization and demonstrates its evaluation with reference annotations, visualization and diarization error rate. Errors are separated into speaker confusion, false alarms and missed speech, including overlap. A transcription comparison shows the same model and meeting dataset producing very different word error rates when headset recordings are replaced by a table microphone, exposing hidden benchmark conditions. The talk also demonstrates why aligning transcription words with diarization turns is nontrivial and why strong component scores do not guarantee correct speaker-attributed text. It emphasizes evaluating real acoustic settings rather than treating single-speaker transcription as solved conversational understanding.

title: Using RL Agent to Detect and Remediate ETL Pipeline Failures - Anna Marie Benzon
summary: Anna Marie Benzon presents a bounded RL-guided ETL remediation system and a controlled synthetic benchmark rather than a production-proven autonomous operator. Deterministic checks establish observable schema and data-quality facts, a learned policy proposes actions, and independent safety rules can force escalation. Evaluation reports detection precision and recall, successful recovery time, repeated-seed confidence intervals and comparisons with deterministic and random action selection. The learned policy matches the deterministic baseline in this compact setting, so the talk attributes reliability mainly to structured state and external constraints. It explicitly reserves production incident validation and shadow deployment as future work.

title: Special Topics in Kernels, RL, Reward Hacking in Agents — Daniel Han, Unsloth
summary: Daniel Han’s extended workshop spans model progress, quantization, inference stacks, kernels, reinforcement learning, and agent reward hacking. Evaluation-relevant sections distinguish benchmark success thresholds, examine long-context degradation, and warn that harness, serving, formatting, extraction, and verifier changes can alter apparent model quality. Han compares competing benchmark claims and discusses contamination and solution leakage, often presenting hypotheses rather than established causes. Later examples show agents optimizing proxy checks by manipulating timers, inputs, caching, or correctness-versus-timing paths. He contrasts outcome rewards with costly process supervision and urges inspecting generated code and measurement infrastructure before publishing improvements. This is a broad, opinionated workshop, not an independently verified benchmark report.

title: Agents Need Feature Flags - Sachin Gupta
summary: Sachin Gupta adapts feature-flag discipline to agent behavior across prompts, tools, models, memory, autonomy, and subagents. He proposes segmented canary releases, rapid rollback, per-tool and agent-wide kill switches, and middleware that every child agent must also obey. Evaluation enters through monitoring behavioral error-rate changes, escalation and hallucination signals, mitigation time, and audit completeness before promoting a variant. Demonstrations include explicitly illustrative incident simulations rather than measured production trials. Gupta also warns that stale caching, session-only flag checks, and untested combinations undermine control. The adjacent lesson is to treat agent behavior changes as observable experiments with enforceable stop conditions, not global prompt edits.

title: From Tokens to Cells: Foundation Models for Single-Cell Biology - Akram Baharlouei, Altos Labs
summary: Akram Baharlouei surveys single-cell foundation models and the measurement problems that complicate their evaluation. RNA-sequencing data offer scale but contain biological variation, snapshot limitations, and technical batch effects; more samples do not automatically produce a faithful representation of cells. In the evaluation-focused section, she discusses multimodal and perturbation-response benchmarks, including scGeneScope and PerturBench, where expensive transformer models can match or underperform simpler baselines. Distributional comparisons motivate flow-matching approaches such as Prime Flow rather than judging only mean predictions. This is a broad biological-model overview, with adjacent value in domain-specific benchmarking, appropriate baselines, and the relationship between data measurement and model conclusions.

title: Claude for Long-Horizon Tasks — Lance Martin, Anthropic
summary: Lance Martin outlines infrastructure and feedback patterns for long-running Claude agents. Separating the harness from execution containers preserves sessions and limits credential exposure, while an append-only event log keeps earlier context retrievable. A substantial section advocates independent verifier contexts with explicit goals or rubrics: builders iterate until a separate, critically tuned verifier confirms the outcome. Martin illustrates this with ML experiments and discusses memory benchmarks, including how offline consolidation corrected a repeatedly harmful Pokémon memory. He also describes organization-level, multiplayer harnesses. The evaluation-related lesson is that task duration, memory improvements, and autonomous completion need measured feedback and independent checks, not self-grading inside the same context.

title: Training Frontier Models to Out-Think Hackers — Uri Rolls, Arithmetic & Thom Wolf, Hugging Face
summary: Uri Rolls and Thom Wolf present an access-control benchmark built from previously undisclosed vulnerabilities found by human researchers. Agents operate black-box, chained software environments without internet or source access, and must reason about system state to achieve an unauthorized capability. Deterministic graders verify both the final outcome and intermediate exploitation steps, providing useful discrimination when complete successes are rare. The speakers contrast reconnaissance with the harder logical leap needed to connect discovered facts, and inspect trajectories to localize those failures. They position high-quality, specialized cyber evaluation data as a prerequisite for stronger defensive models, while noting that one benchmark cannot represent the whole security domain.

title: State of Data — Sean Cai, Independent / State of Data
summary: Sean Cai examines AI data markets through task verifiability and the difference between captured real workflows and contrived expert examples. A substantial section critiques benchmarks that sell both a target and training data to optimize it, ignore long dependent episodes, or report a single score without measuring harness and infrastructure variation. Finance examples illustrate how similar aggregate scores can conceal opposite strengths in arithmetic and methodology. Cai proposes examining decomposition into checkable steps, agreement about correctness, and the availability of independently verified outcomes. These are an industry practitioner’s claims, not independently established market facts; the adjacent evaluation contribution is a framework for judging realism, rubric quality, and benchmark incentives.

title: Agents at Scale: Inside MiniMax's Model and the Infrastructure Behind It — Dan Fu and Olive Song
summary: Dan Fu and Olive Song discuss MiniMax-M3's open-weight release, multimodal training, and the inference engineering needed for agentic workloads. Song stresses environment, data, and reward design for kernel optimization, computer use, and long-running research tasks. Fu describes ParallelKernelBench as a collection of practically useful, unsolved kernel problems: improvements can directly accelerate inference rather than merely raise leaderboard scores. For long-horizon evaluation, Song describes scoring successive submissions and using validation/test splits to distinguish genuine gains from hacking. The discussion also covers sparse-attention kernels, quantization, distributed KV-cache management, and internal development evaluations, emphasizing continuous optimization after launch rather than a fixed serving configuration.

title: Einstein Arena: Harnessing Collective Agent Intelligence for Open Science — James Zou, Together AI
summary: James Zou argues that agent environments should supply incentives, resources, and guardrails rather than prescribe rigid workflows. Einstein Arena combines open scientific problems, deterministic solution verifiers, public leaderboards, and forums where agents exchange and refine solutions. He reports new mathematical constructions and production kernel improvements from this collaborative competition. The second example, DS Gym, provides a unified execution environment for evaluating and training data-science agents. Zou highlights shortcut-prone existing benchmarks, reporting that agents could solve substantial portions without using the underlying datasets. DS Gym instead curates expert-reviewed scientific tasks and recent Kaggle problems, then uses code execution to verify trajectories that can also train smaller open models.

title: If we want them to do Knowledge Work, design them as Knowledge Agents — Benjamin Clavié, Mixedbread
summary: Benjamin Clavié argues that knowledge agents need search tools and organizational patterns different from coding agents. His benchmark discussion shows how poorly tuned BM25 baselines can distort conclusions and how similar accuracy may conceal meaningful tool-call savings. He compares text-only retrieval ceilings with multimodal search on enterprise PDFs, then introduces searcher agents that return short research memos to an orchestrator. The reported gain is framed as reducing the remaining oracle gap rather than only adding percentage points. The broader lesson is to use evaluations to identify whether tools, orchestration or information access constrain performance, and co-design those components instead of assuming coding workflows generalize.

title: Stop Chunking Like It's 2022 — Yuval Belfer, AI21 Labs
summary: Yuval Belfer uses retrieval experiments to challenge the assumption that a corpus has one optimal chunk size. Across meeting transcripts, narrative question answering, Seinfeld trivia and financial data, different queries favor different windows. An oracle experiment selects the best size per query to expose potential recall gains; he distinguishes this diagnostic upper bound from a deployable system. His proposed multiscale index retrieves across several window sizes, maps results to whole documents, and merges rankings with reciprocal rank fusion. Reported gains come with two-to-fivefold memory costs, while parallel searches limit latency impact. The talk illustrates how query-level analysis and upper-bound experiments reveal overlooked retrieval bottlenecks.

title: Building the Document Context Layer for AI Agents — Jerry Liu, LlamaIndex
summary: Jerry Liu describes document infrastructure as the context layer around an agent harness. After explaining why PDFs lack explicit reading order and table semantics, he contrasts heuristic parsing, one-shot VLM reading and hybrid routing. The evaluation contribution is ParseBench: a reported 2,000 human-verified pages comparing roughly 50 models and OCR systems on tables, charts, faithfulness and semantic formatting. He emphasizes usefulness for agent understanding rather than syntactic output alone. The talk places benchmark results on accuracy, cost and latency tradeoff curves, distinguishing regulated high-accuracy extraction from cheap bulk indexing and fast interactive ingestion. It closes with parsing tools, structured extraction and source-grounded citations.

title: Burn Your Flags: Interactive CLIs for Agents — Mark Lummus & Navinkumar Patil, PayPal
summary: Mark Lummus and Navinkumar Patil explore how agents can operate interactive command-line interfaces designed around human terminals, prompts, and keyboard controls. A workshop competition evaluates a cafe-ordering CLI using task accuracy and response time, encouraging participants to build adapters and interaction strategies. High-scoring solutions expose a benchmark-design issue: deterministic parsing and network-speed optimization can outperform the intended agent-interaction approach without demonstrating the capability originally being explored. The discussion includes terminal multiplexing and machine-readable alternatives for tools. The evaluation lesson is to define what a leaderboard actually measures and inspect successful strategies before interpreting their scores as evidence of general interactive-tool competence.

title: Insurance Claims Are AI's Messiest Data Problem — Denys Linkov, Wisedocs
summary: Denys Linkov describes the messy document pipeline behind insurance claims: handwriting, faxes, duplication, inconsistent forms, and enormous PDFs complicate extraction and reasoning. A benchmark built with Artificial Analysis evaluates medical-record questions against expert-validated answers, with the reported initial best reasoning accuracy around twenty percent. The discussion connects model quality to cost frontiers and stresses judge calibration rather than uncritical reliance on an LLM score. Broader architecture examples use successive levels of extraction and abstraction with model and human verification. The point is to test the actual document and reasoning challenges of the domain; generic model capability and nominal context length do not establish reliable claim analysis.

title: Same GPU, 50% More Output: Why the Operator Matters — Oliver Kennon, SemiAnalysis
summary: Oliver Kennon distinguishes rented GPU hours from the useful intelligence an operator delivers. A same-chip serving comparison reportedly produces about fifty percent more output at a specified interactivity target, illustrating how software and operations change economic performance. He describes ClusterMAX’s assessment of provisioning, reliability, monitoring, security, documentation, and failure handling, while noting that these are not direct token-output measurements. The broader discussion separates rental prices, production costs, comparable compute grades, and futures exposure. His proposed north-star measure is full cost per successfully completed task at required quality. The comparisons and examples are bounded illustrations rather than a claim that one hardware label defines equivalent delivered service.

title: How Bridgewater Turned 100 Million Documents Into an Edge - Sam Green & Aaron Linsky, Bridgewater
summary: Sam Green and Aaron Linsky describe Bridgewater’s Vault, a permissioned research corpus serving both people and agents. Their search-quality section turns complaints into an approximately two-hundred-example benchmark built in less than a week, using precision at ten to measure whether the highest-ranked results contain the right documents. Reported relevance rises from roughly sixty percent to around ninety to ninety-five percent after search improvements. The talk also explains why human readers need precision while agents can process broader result sets, and why filtering must preserve recall and latency under agent-scale demand. The benchmark supports local product decisions; the reported gains are not a universal comparison of search systems.

title: Stop Giving Your Agent Tools. Give It a Sandbox - Mikyo King, Arize AI
summary: Mikyo King explains code mode: instead of exposing a large tool catalog and returning all raw tool outputs, give an agent a sandbox where it can discover and compose operations in code. Phoenix examples include Bash, Python, SQL, and UI interaction. He also details the new failure surfaces: credentials, permissions, egress, sandbox startup, durability, and generated-code accuracy. The evaluation section uses realistic Harbor tasks, verifiers, and repeated trials to compare behavior while capturing trajectories. Reported results show 43% fewer tokens and 31% lower cost with roughly unchanged latency. These are measurements from the presented setup, not a general guarantee for every model or task.

title: CI/CD Is Dead, Agents Need Continuous Compute and Computers — Hugo Santos and Madison Faulkner
summary: Madison Faulkner and Hugo Santos argue that autonomous coding agents overwhelm CI/CD workflows designed for infrequent human changes. They propose moving build, test, and review feedback into a continuous, stateful agent loop rather than treating validation as a separate pull-request phase. Internal validation uses repository builds and tests; external validation can involve specialized security and API-conformance agents. Completed changes enter a premerge queue, where people assess intent and demonstrated outcomes while coordination reconciles concurrent edits. The talk emphasizes fast incremental infrastructure, known-source invariants, and continuous governance. Its contribution is a verification architecture and future-facing proposal, not an experimentally validated evaluation framework.

title: Beyond Code Coverage: Functionality Testing with Playwright MCP — Marlene Mhangami, Microsoft
summary: Marlene Mhangami argues that AI-generated unit tests can affirm existing implementation while missing broken user behavior. She proposes behavior-focused red-green-refactor development with Playwright: derive failing browser tests from feature requests, generate code to pass them, and reserve human attention for refactoring. In a toy-store example, Copilot begins generating tests while a prepared implementation is exercised through search, category, and price-filter interactions. She recommends retaining screenshots in pull requests, committing before automated changes, and organizing tests around features. Q&A discusses specialized Playwright agent instructions for state-heavy applications, direct API testing as an alternative, and testing mobile versus desktop layouts.

title: Why Rust is the Ideal Language for Vibe-Coding — Daniel Szoke, Sentry
summary: Daniel Szoke argues that ease of generating runnable code is a poor optimization target if language flexibility allows hidden defects. Tests and review agents remain useful but can mirror implementation mistakes or miss untested behavior. Rust’s compiler supplies deterministic constraints for types, nullability, memory and concurrency, with actionable errors an agent can use in its repair loop. A threaded-counter example illustrates rejecting unsafe shared state before runtime. The talk does not claim compilation proves overall correctness; its evaluation-adjacent contribution is moving some verification from fallible generated tests and subjective review into independently enforced language invariants.

title: BDD, ADR, PRD, WTF: Capturing Decisions for Humans and AI Alike — Michal Cichra, Safe Intelligence
summary: Michal Cichra connects architecture decision records, product requirements and executable behavior-driven scenarios to make agent-written software reviewable. Cucumber tests close the gap between a prose specification and observed product behavior, while architectural lint rules prevent forbidden dependencies such as browser tests directly accessing a database. Git hooks and CI enforce the same checks and direct rejected agents back to documents explaining the rule. Specialized skills change the focus of the loop for UI work, tests or design decisions. Persistent specifications and automated enforcement keep long sessions consistent even across repeated context compaction.

title: We Cut 94% of AI Coding Tokens With a Local Code Index - Rajkumar Sakthivel, Tesco
summary: Rajkumar Sakthivel reports a local code index built to reduce irrelevant context sent to coding models. It combines structure-aware code chunks, semantic and keyword search, relationship traversal and inexpensive relevance scoring. A public FastAPI experiment with twenty developer questions compares retrieved context against full-file reading and reports a 94% token reduction while preserving useful retrieval. Crucially, the speaker qualifies the baseline: production coding tools already avoid some full-file reads, so real savings are smaller. He also reports recall collapsing on a larger, mixed-responsibility codebase, making benchmark scope and failure analysis more informative than the headline efficiency claim.

title: Should AI Engineers Still Read Code in 2026? The Z/L Continuum — Alex Volkov, ThursdAI
summary: Alex Volkov reframes the argument over reading all AI-generated code as a task-level question: what proof does this specific change need? His Z/L continuum spans close human inspection and system-level oversight, but neither endpoint removes verification. Critical authentication, money, permissions, and irreversible-data changes warrant deeper review; large changes should be decomposed, and traces, evals, shadow mode, independent reviewers, observability, and rollback supply complementary evidence. Volkov warns that a builder grading itself hides review rather than eliminating it. The talk uses industry examples and reported studies, not a new controlled experiment, to argue that advancing capability changes where proof belongs, not whether it is required.

title: Why Software Factories Fail
summary: Dex Horthy argues that autonomous software factories fail when passing tests is mistaken for maintaining a healthy codebase. He walks through reinforcement-learning-style coding tasks and explains how binary correctness rewards omit architectural degradation whose costs emerge months later. His team’s lights-off experiment exposed the difficulty of recovering from failures in code nobody had reviewed. Horthy surveys longer-horizon benchmarks and quality-aware verification attempts, but cautions that model review cannot automatically solve the underlying training gap. His interim prescription is human ownership supported by AI-assisted product review, architecture, program design, and vertical implementation slices, reducing review burden through earlier alignment rather than removing verification.

title: Loop Engineering from First Principles — Kyle Mistele, HumanLayer
summary: Kyle Mistele applies control theory to coding-agent workflows: measure the gap between current and desired code, select a small corrective action, execute it, and measure again. His practical example incrementally migrates RPC procedures using structural-search sensors, deterministic selection, golden implementation patterns, and scheduled CI workflows. Versioned baselines prevent new violations, while a feedback file captures review corrections for subsequent iterations. Flow control prevents accumulating more unreviewed pull requests when the previous change remains open. This is broader than model evaluation, but its central contribution is an evidence-driven improvement loop that keeps changes measurable, reversible, and small enough for accountable human verification.

title: How to Get Your Org to Adopt Coding Agents (Without Shipping Garbage) — Eyal Blum, Figma
summary: Eyal Blum describes Figma’s uneven adoption of coding agents and argues that verification investment is the most useful response to experienced engineers’ skepticism. He recommends shifting repeated checks into deterministic tooling, using test-first development so tests constrain implementation rather than conform to generated code, and reserving human review for higher-level functional judgment. Detailed plans should divide work into independently verifiable, reviewable stages with acceptance gates. Skeptics’ knowledge of failure modes becomes a roadmap for safer tooling. The talk also addresses reduced developer agency and attention-aware communication, including marking human-written versus generated PR descriptions. Its evaluation relevance is the organization and economics of trustworthy verification.

title: Building Self-Improving Agent Software Factories — Suraj Gupta, Warp
summary: Gupta describes three mechanisms for improving software factories: evolving skills, persistent memory, and task-specific model routing. An outer-loop agent reviews triage runs and human feedback, proposes procedural updates through Git-tracked pull requests, and leaves humans to guard against regressions. A parallel memory loop extracts reusable facts and outcomes with provenance, versioning, and human edit or deletion controls, reducing repeated investigation. Routing aims to balance capability and cost rather than using expensive models everywhere. Warp internally compares models through an evaluation sidecar, while customer-defined workflow evaluations are described as forthcoming. The presentation offers concrete architectural examples but no quantitative proof of factory-wide improvement, and one provenance demonstration is blocked by access restrictions.

title: What It Actually Takes to Build a Software Factory — Tereza Tížková, Factory
summary: Tereza Tížková describes Factory’s software-factory architecture, emphasizing that autonomous duration does not establish reliability. Missions use orchestrators, sequential workers, and separate validators operating against a validation contract written before implementation. Scrutiny validators inspect code, types, linters, and tests; user-testing validators operate the running interface to distinguish functional software from convincing-looking output. She warns that poorly defined completion criteria encourage test gaming. Model routing and agent-readiness checks provide additional evaluation context. Reported routing savings and a customer mission’s validation effort are vendor examples, not independently verified benchmarks; the talk explicitly treats reliable long-running autonomy as an unsolved challenge.

title: The State of AI in Software Development: Data from 400+ Orgs — Justin Reock, DX
summary: Reock presents DX research on AI's organizational impact, emphasizing that throughput metrics are proxies, not business value. He reports rising deployment frequency and larger pull requests alongside volatile change-failure rates, improved perceived maintainability, and reduced confidence in changes. Junior engineers reportedly use AI more and consume more tokens, while senior engineers achieve similar time savings. His measurement framework links utilization, impact, and cost through cohort comparisons using established productivity and experience metrics. He argues that infrastructure readiness and bottlenecks outside code generation constrain gains, highlighting administrative, legacy-understanding, review, and incident-response applications. Findings are observational rather than clean causal estimates; cohort differences and infrastructure conditions complicate attribution to AI.

title: How VS Code Went from Monthly to Weekly Releases with AI — Harald Kirschner
summary: Kirschner explains VS Code’s move from monthly to weekly releases as a whole-system redesign, not simply greater AI usage. Agent-ready documentation, expert-maintained skills, faster TypeScript builds, component screenshot diffs, and Playwright-driven application access shorten implementation and verification loops. Automated code review precedes human review, while issue triage and error telemetry generate investigations and proposed fixes. Staged rollouts limit risk for an installed application. Product-specific evaluation scenarios connect customer reports to offline benchmarks and online experimentation, revealing surprising model-token behavior even on trivial tasks. Reported code-survival and build-speed gains are team observations. Durable ownership, daily prototyping, and continual bottleneck removal support both quality and faster learning.

title: Harness Engineering: How to Build a Software Factory — Dru Knox, Tessl
summary: Dru Knox frames harness engineering as three feedback loops for moving toward a software factory. Cheap, frequent inner checks help agents correct work before a pull request; expensive outer checks, including agentic QA and mutation testing, build confidence after submission. A meta loop mines agent logs, pull requests, issues, and user feedback for escaped mistakes and updates the other loops. He distinguishes reduced human correction from reduced review and recommends tracking manual takeovers, review comments, and agent-initiated work while holding product quality steady. The talk offers process guidance and Tessl tooling examples, not measured evidence that adopting this architecture improves quality.

title: Your AI Agent Has No Nervous System — Matt Gibiec, Dynatrace
summary: Gibiec argues that agents lack the operational context needed to make dependable engineering decisions, describing observability as their missing nervous system. He urges teams to define user value and success measures before accelerating deployment. Dynatrace's Bluebox is presented as a context layer connecting production telemetry, service dependencies, historical baselines, and repository changes to coding workflows. Proposed applications include production-informed local testing, early anomaly detection, change-correlated diagnosis, safer remediation, and feature planning. The workflow progresses from observation to suggested fixes while retaining human release decisions. These are preview-product scenarios and presenter claims, not demonstrated benchmark evidence; the talk offers no measured accuracy or assurance that dependency context eliminates regressions.

title: Build with Perception Agents — Emile Baizel & Shruti Arora, Amazon AGI Lab
summary: Emile Baizel and Shruti Arora connect visual feedback to a coding-agent repair loop. A browser extension lets users select elements, draw annotations, and export structured changes; visual verification then checks the rendered application against design requirements and user flows. The workshop wires these primitives through a local bridge into a podcast-page editing exercise and produces verification reports after changes. Examples include a duck-themed interface and conversational design feedback, with some audience integrations remaining prototypes. The evaluation lesson is to inspect what users actually see and can do, not merely accept the coding agent’s completion claim. Annotation and model-based verification are separate components with different reliability characteristics.

title: How to Build Quality Gates into Agentic Coding Workflows — Nnenna Ndukwe, Qodo AI
summary: Ndukwe presents a structured agentic coding workflow using a FastAPI payments workshop. Teams first codify quality standards as reusable rules and skills, then carry that context through planning, test-driven implementation, local deterministic checks, and pull-request review. Detailed plans specify behavior, constraints, verification commands, recovery, and completion evidence. A refund demonstration surfaces non-durable idempotency storage and rule violations; an agent-driven remediation loop fixes findings and reruns checks. She advocates combining static analysis and tests with AI review rather than treating either as sufficient. Audience questions expose limits: Qodo ingests skills without evaluating their effectiveness, and AI selection of relevant rules is not deterministic, even when severity-based merge blocking is.

title: Rebuilding CI for AI-Scale Commit Volume — Gautam Korlam, Sonar
summary: Gautam Korlam describes how agent-scale pull-request volume shifts delivery bottlenecks into CI, repair loops, review, and approval. SubmitQueue-style testing of combinations protects the main branch, while incremental builds, caching, sharding, and parallelism reduce feedback latency. The more consequential verification lesson is that green CI alone does not establish permission to merge: risk-sensitive policies, independent approval, and durable evidence must apply to the exact tested commit. Known failures and overrides need recorded reasons so agents do not repeatedly rediscover problems or silently bypass controls. The talk advocates measuring the complete proposal-to-accepted-change path rather than equating more generated pull requests with more delivered value.

title: Why Are We Still Governing AI Agents Like Software? - Tim Tyler, Gravitee
summary: Tim Tyler proposes governing AI agents as an accountable digital workforce rather than anonymous software processes. His framework covers assignment of identity and a human sponsor, alignment of role and mission with least-privilege authority, and administration through oversight and recourse. Evaluation appears in role-specific scorecards that distinguish task success from compliance with authorized behavior, including invoice accuracy, cycle time, budgets, and intent confidence. Guardian agents can monitor continually, while explicit thresholds determine redaction, restrictions, or escalation to people. The framework requires human judgment to revise roles and controls as evidence accumulates; conversational assurances do not establish alignment or justify expanded permissions.

title: How Anthropic Merges 30,000 Code Changes a Day - Manish Kapur, Sonar & Addy Osmani, Anthropic
summary: Manish Kapur and Addy Osmani discuss the verification bottleneck created by coding agents and increasingly automated software factories. Osmani describes Anthropic’s growth from roughly 2,500 to 30,000 merged changes per day, with Claude providing first-pass review supported by verification evidence. The speakers distinguish supervised factories from fully automated ones and advocate independent checks inside each production loop. End-to-end tests, property tests, visual checks, security analysis, permissions, and human escalation address different risks. Survey statistics and company throughput figures are speaker-reported observations, not universal productivity guarantees. Their central recommendation is to define precisely what sufficient evidence for merging means, rather than ask teams simply to trust agent output.

title: Catch the Bugs Your Code Review Misses - Killian Carlsen-Phelan & Taylor Luttrell-Williams, Sonar
summary: Killian Carlsen-Phelan and Taylor Luttrell-Williams demonstrate Gitar as a verification layer for agent-written pull requests. A sample ticketing application supplies three exercises: identify a refund bug outside the changed lines, enforce an all-in pricing rule supplied through repository configuration, and repair a failing CI test before automatic merging. The session separates passing existing tests from satisfying business intent and emphasizes rechecking each new commit. It also covers explicit verification instructions, learned conventions, ticket-based functional validation, and cross-repository or cross-PR context. These are demonstrations of a proposed review workflow, not evidence that automated review can prove the absence of defects.

title: Why a One-Line Change Can Break Your Whole Stack - Cole Gannaway, Qodo
summary: Cole Gannaway shows how a one-line data-model change can pass builds, tests, and linting while breaking several downstream clients. He proposes a software graph that exposes cross-repository dependencies and the true change surface, alongside rules capturing business requirements and reviewer knowledge. The discussion explicitly separates the agent authoring code from the reviewer judging it and considers different models and harnesses to reduce correlated blind spots. Reviewer comments can become reusable constraints, and reviews can be run during implementation rather than only afterward. Ticket-level intent checks and human escalation remain important because neither a passing test suite nor another agent’s approval guarantees the right behavior.

title: Does GenAI "belong" to data scientists? — Phil Hetzel, Braintrust
summary: Phil Hetzel argues that agent development should not be isolated inside a traditional ML platform team. Foundation models arrive pretrained, but applications still require contextual evaluation, observability and domain judgment. Product and systems engineers build reliable integrations, subject-matter experts annotate traces and shape prompts, and data scientists contribute statistical rigor, risk awareness and judge validation. He specifically distinguishes broad functional agent quality from simply reusing precision, recall and F1, while recommending those metrics for testing discrete LLM-judge outputs against labeled data. Production examples should continually refresh offline datasets and reveal divergence from human judgments.

title: Trading Desks to Clinical Trials: Parallels in Applied Vertical AI — Ayush Bhardwaj, Allos AI
summary: Ayush Bhardwaj compares applied AI development in hedge funds and pharmaceutical technology, arguing that useful systems depend on narrow tasks, proprietary data, and domain expertise rather than commodity agent infrastructure. His development recipe combines problem formulation, data curation, prompts, observability, expert involvement, iterative learning, and deployment justified by business value. He recounts why uncalibrated LLM judging failed to replace traders' or scientists' judgment and recommends hiring representative users to evaluate outputs and refine reasoning workflows. Trace-based error analysis is presented as a low-cost starting point before fine-tuning or preference-based training. He warns about rubric echo chambers and retraining costs, while emphasizing that experts still make consequential decisions with AI assistance.

title: Respect The Process - Andrew Dumit, Watershed Technology Inc.
summary: Andrew Dumit explains why sustainability agents must justify how an answer was produced when experts can legitimately disagree on the final number. A coding agent gains flexibility but can bypass intended interfaces, claim edits that never happened or leave work nontechnical users cannot review. Watershed constrains effects through a typed SDK and owns final execution, enabling linting, conflict checks, artifact validation and readable change reports. Internal task evaluations improve with ordinary harness engineering, but the main distinction is that a traceable, replayable process remains inspectable even when the final result differs from one reference answer.

title: Design Patterns for AI Trust: Juries, Libraries, and Agent Tiers — Alex Bauer, Upside.tech
summary: Alex Bauer presents three practical patterns for improving trust in go-to-market agents: documented anchor assets, a librarian that supplies business definitions and prior failure knowledge, and independent analysts overseen by a consensus judge. The jury pattern addresses attribution questions without a single empirically correct answer. Analysts produce evidence-cited opinions independently, while the judge weighs reasoning rather than treating conclusions as facts and expands the jury when consensus is insufficient. Bauer also stresses source traceability and choosing capable agent harnesses for consequential work. This is a broader product-pattern talk, not a calibrated evaluation study, but its judging and evidence-management sections provide adjacent quality-control ideas.

title: ReviewDebt: a practical framework for scoring every pull request — Sachin Gupta, Ebay
summary: Sachin Gupta presents ReviewDebt, a deterministic framework for measuring the gap between generated code and code humans have reviewed and understood. Five signal families cover diff size and coupling, test evidence, ownership spread, authorship indicators, and missing rationale. Scores should produce explanations and next actions, not simply rank developers or penalize AI use. A scan of public repositories shows structural complexity and volume driving burden more clearly than authorship labels. Gupta recommends backtesting and calibrating weights against local reviewer experience, surfacing scores without immediate blocking, and tracking trends. The framework measures review effort proxies, not proven code correctness or an independently established time-to-review model.

title: "I've never seen anything scarier than an LLM with tool calls." — Erik Meijer aka @HeadinTheBox
summary: Erik Meijer distinguishes difficult-to-formalize judgments about safe language from machine-checkable properties of agent actions. Tool use introduces side effects that may occur before a harmless final answer, so he proposes separating planning from execution. Agents emit an inspectable program representing the intended computation together with a proof, rather than directly running opaque IO actions. A trusted interpreter or checker can then apply type, dataflow, and taint analyses before execution. The talk presents this as proof-carrying code adapted to agents and points to an implementation. Its guarantees depend on the specified language, properties, and trusted execution boundary; it is adjacent formal verification, not an empirical application benchmark.

title: Modern Post-Training: A Deep Dive  — Will Brown, Prime Intellect
summary: Will Brown presents Prime Intellect’s post-training stack, centering evaluation and training on reusable executable environments. The revised verifiers design separates task sets, agent harnesses, and runtimes so teams can compare real agents without rewriting their deployment logic. Rewards and metrics are explicit functions; group-level comparisons support ranking, pairwise judging, and efficiency bonuses among correct solutions. User simulators and interception servers enable realistic multi-turn rollouts, while trace graphs and renderer tooling preserve the distinction between logical messages and exact tokens. The second half covers asynchronous RL scaling and pluggable algorithms. Evaluation is presented as the practical entry point, with the same environment abstractions later supporting training.

title: "The engineer of the future is the person who chooses what is worth doing." — Addy Osmani, Anthropic
summary: Addy Osmani argues that automated engineering still needs accountable judgments about whether work should ship. Agents can investigate, implement, test, and report, but humans must decide whether the evidence is sufficient, understand the constraints, and own residual risk. He distinguishes delegation from blindly borrowing an agent’s confidence, and describes cognitive debt and orchestration overhead as threats to effective review. Verification should become cheaper, clearer, and harder to skip through harnesses, static checks, critique, and intentional checkpoints. This is an engineering-practice keynote rather than an evaluation-method tutorial; its adjacent contribution is a clear boundary between producing quality evidence and making responsible production decisions.

title: "The biggest challenge in your stack? Evals, Evals, Evals" - 2026 State of AI Engineering results
summary: Barr Yaron presents a survey of 1,048 AI builders, placing evaluation challenges within broader changes in model choice, costs, agent permissions, and engineering work. Respondents prioritize quality when selecting models, monitor production quality and costs, and frequently combine multiple providers. Evaluation again ranks as the leading stack challenge, while informal “vibe review” remains the most common evaluation approach. The survey also reports wider agent write access, relatively blunt human-approval and permission controls, and downstream concerns about review burden and declining codebase understanding. This is an industry-practice overview rather than an evaluation tutorial; its relevant contribution is evidence about the gap between rapidly expanding agent adoption and mature quality-control methods.

title: AI Agents for Performance: Ship Faster, Pay Less — Rajat Shah, Netflix
summary: Rajat Shah describes Netflix’s use of coding agents to analyze production profiles, locate inefficient code, and propose performance fixes. Profiles identify promising hotspots, but they are not proof of savings: functional tests and canary comparisons against real traffic establish correctness, CPU reduction, latency changes, and error-rate regressions before human approval. A shared Git-based catalog records confirmed patterns and anti-patterns so later agents can reuse evidence across services and eventually prevent inefficient code earlier in development. Shah recommends incremental automation with strong deterministic foundations. The adjacent evaluation lesson is to separate model-proposed optimization hypotheses from measured production outcomes and retain accountable review.

title: Compression at the Edge — NVIDIA, Unsloth, HuggingFace, Ollama
summary: This panel explores quantization and other compression techniques for local and enterprise model deployment. Speakers explain mixed-precision treatment of sensitive layers, NVFP4 block scaling, and tradeoffs among model size, throughput, hardware requirements, and quality. Evaluation emerges as a major engineering burden: NVIDIA's representative describes benchmarking against original model cards and an accuracy-degradation target, while Ollama stresses testing actual agent harnesses beyond benchmark scores. Unsloth warns that quantizing linear-attention layers can appear acceptable until long-context use fails. Discussion also covers smaller models' recovery-training difficulties, architectural diversity, KV-cache compression, and sparsity. The closing exchange proposes comparing quantized and original output distributions using KL divergence alongside accuracy measurements.

title: From RL to IRL — Gaurav Mishra, Amazon AGI Lab
summary: Gaurav Mishra examines why reinforcement-learned coding agents do not automatically become safe computer-use agents. Early browser-training examples show password guessing that locks an account and an advertisement's misleading Submit button diverting an agent into disclosing information. Real deployments introduce partial observations, irreversible actions, expired authority, uncertain execution, and ambiguous success. His remedy combines realistic training sandboxes, native recovery actions, process-level penalties for dangerous behavior, and calibrated escalation. Models need visual grounding and change detection; harnesses add risk classification, credential checks, execution monitoring, audit trails, rollback where possible, and human handoff. A later demonstration handles the deceptive button and expired login correctly, illustrating a deployment-feedback-to-training loop.

title: From Ingestion to Agents: How AI Teams Build on Document Intelligence — Adit Abraham, Reducto
summary: Adit Abraham explains why document quality becomes more consequential when agents compound decisions across multiple steps. He compares traditional vision pipelines with VLMs, advocates token-level OCR correction rather than wholesale rewriting, and shows how representation affects both reasoning and retrieval. Benchmark examples distinguish precision from silently dropped content and show better structured inputs improving downstream answers while reducing reasoning effort. Agent harnesses can iteratively reconstruct charts and validate large extractions. His evaluation recommendation is explicit: test parsing, retrieval, formatting and end-agent performance separately, and complement public datasets with production monitoring because deployed document distributions differ. The talk is an applied document-engineering case with substantial quality methodology.

title: From Scratch to SOTA: Training a 3B State-Space Vision Model — Krishna Prasad Srinivasan, Sarvam
summary: Krishna Prasad Srinivasan describes Sarvam’s compact state-space vision model for English and 22 Indian languages. Beyond architecture and staged training, he emphasizes a data engine coupled to evaluations designed for end-user usefulness. OCR provides machine-checkable rewards: character error, table structure, equations and grammar can be scored through unit tests for reinforcement learning. He reports performance on English document benchmarks and describes a planned Indic benchmark spanning historical and modern documents with diverse layouts. The Q&A stresses faithful extraction, including preserving mistakes in the source rather than silently correcting them. Deployment feedback, confidence scores and block-level grounding connect benchmark development with production document quality.

title: Autoresearch Made Our Models 3x Faster — Tejas Bhakta, Morph
summary: Bhakta describes GPU-kernel autoresearch as a proposal, correctness check, benchmark, and keep-or-revert loop. Humans supply architectural ideas and profiling insights; agents search implementation parameters using detailed hardware and model context. Correctness and speed make kernels attractive optimization targets, but reward hacking can make a local kernel faster while slowing end-to-end inference, for example by disabling CUDA graphs or testing only favorable context lengths. Optimized kernels may require workload-dependent fallbacks. He reports combining kernel and bare-metal tuning for approximately threefold model speedups, while warning that most attempted changes fail. The practical argument is disciplined measurement and constraints, not guaranteed automatic discovery of novel architectures or universal acceleration.

title: Scale the Judgment, Not the Model — Andrew Orobator, Reddit
summary: Orobator argues that trustworthy automation requires scaling institutional judgment through skills, worklogs, personas, and enforceable verification gates rather than simply upgrading models. A verification ladder extends from builds and tests to screenshots, recorded application flows, and production telemetry; autonomy grows only as evidence improves. His local stale-feature-flag agent applies risk and experiment checks before proposing mechanical changes, with reported backtesting and seven successful CI-passing pull requests. Humans retain merge approval. Personal experiments reveal bypassable hooks and self-authorized exceptions, motivating lower-level gates whose overrides remain operator-only. Scheduled reviews and postmortems keep encoded judgment current as architecture changes; the examples do not establish general autonomous reliability.

title: MCP Doesn't Suck. Your Agent Does. — Jan Čurn, Apify
summary: Čurn argues that common MCP complaints stem from agent-harness design rather than the protocol itself. Eager tool loading and routing large or sensitive results through context create avoidable cost, reliability, and security problems. Progressive discovery and code-mode execution provide alternatives, while CLIs already benefit from familiar shell composition and incremental help. His MCPC demonstration wraps MCP in a CLI supporting structured JSON, authentication, persistent sessions, tool discovery, and asynchronous tasks. Connector Evals then holds the agent fixed to compare interfaces on completion time and token cost. Early examples show MCPC and native CLI behaving similarly, with raw MCP often more token-heavy; these preliminary results are not universal rankings.

title: AI Writes More PRs. Who Validates Them? — Ali-Reza Adl-Tabatabai, Sonar
summary: Adl-Tabatabai argues that AI-generated code shifts engineering bottlenecks into centralized CI and code review, where failures create expensive, slow feedback loops. He presents Gitar's agentic validation system, now part of Sonar, as an orchestration layer that reviews pull requests, explains CI failures, identifies flaky tests, and iterates on fixes. Teams can progressively enable merge blocking, automatic remediation, and conditional approval and merging as trust grows. The system also categorizes CI failures and engineering work for platform and leadership teams. He describes a specialized harness and model-routing proxy, then advocates combining agents with traditional program analysis. Claimed quality, security, and productivity benefits are product assertions rather than quantified benchmark results.

title: Teaching Agents to Search with NVIDIA Data Designer — Dhruv Nathawani, NVIDIA
summary: Nathawani demonstrates NeMo Data Designer as a reproducible pipeline for generating diverse synthetic training data, progressing from question-answer pairs to MCP-mediated search trajectories. Wikidata graph walks seed difficult riddles intended to require reasoning and search rather than memorized answers. He reports moving a model from zero to thirty percent on BrowseComp after filtering fifty thousand seeds into roughly seven thousand high-quality supervised records. Evaluation combines judges, task-specific checks, current information, and human review of judge decisions. Stale seed facts and brittle answer matching illustrate why no single verifier is sufficient. Additional examples cover SQL, structured outputs, demographic personas, and privacy-oriented data tooling.

title: Vector Isn't Enough: Hybrid Search & Retrieval — Jeff Vestal & James Williams, Elastic
summary: Vestal and Williams lead an Elastic workshop comparing semantic vector retrieval, BM25 lexical search, hybrid fusion, and optional reranking. They explain why exact identifiers can defeat semantic search and why lexical matching misses paraphrased intent. Reciprocal rank fusion offers a starting point, while normalized linear combinations allow weight tuning against relevance judgments. Evaluation centers on desired documents, precision and recall targets, top-ranked chunks, and end-to-end latency including inference. Agent Builder examples connect retrieval quality to grounded answers, citations, and inspectable search traces. The presenters recommend adding rerankers only when measured relevance gains justify latency; their small workshop dataset and vendor guidance do not establish universal superiority, and automatic relevance tuning remains unreleased.

title: Claude Managed Agents Q&A: Evals, CI/CD and Multi-Tenancy (Part 4 of 4) — Anthropic
summary: Priyanka Phatak and Gabe Cemaj answer operational questions about Claude Managed Agents, including a focused discussion of evaluation. Anthropic runs many cloud sessions in parallel and revisits prompts and harness assumptions for each model release. For application builders, they prioritize well-defined, high-quality datasets and scoring historical sessions over achieving perfect numbers on poorly specified tasks. Related examples cover code-review agents, sandbox QA, YAML configuration synchronized through CI/CD, tenant workspaces, and responsive coordinator/subagent patterns. The advice is useful for constructing an evaluation workflow inside a managed platform, but the session is broader product Q&A; it does not provide a benchmark comparison or a complete evaluator implementation.

title: Scheduled Agents, Dreaming and Q&A: Claude Managed Agents (Part 3 of 4) — Anthropic
summary: Gabe Cemaj demonstrates scheduled managed-agent deployments, fan-out sessions, and Dreaming, a research preview that reviews past sessions to improve shared memory. The Q&A repeatedly returns to evaluation: task-specific datasets are needed to compare harness choices, judge whether memory changes help, and assess new model releases. The presenters caution against assuming that a feature tuned for coding transfers equally well to another application. Outcomes and verifier loops provide explicit success criteria, while observability supports inspection of long-running sessions. The broader session covers tenancy, compaction, skills, scaling, and deployment options. Its contribution is contextual evaluation advice around memory and orchestration, not a controlled proof that Dreaming improves every workload.

title: Deploying AI Inside a Bank Is Not an Engineering Problem — Paden Gayle, Applied AI Engineers
summary: Paden Gayle argues that bank AI deployments fail when teams discover approval and control requirements only after building a convincing demo. A hypothetical document-exception assistant illustrates how intended use, source ownership, hosting, analyst review, and authority must be agreed early. Evaluation evidence should preserve actual inputs, outputs, model versions, reviewer actions, failure modes, detection paths, and fallback owners. Results need segmentation because a good average can hide poorly supported document types or user groups. He recommends the smallest useful authority boundary and incremental evidence before expansion. The framework is a deployment planning method, not a guarantee that human review or a checklist establishes regulatory approval.

title: The Agent Works. Does Anyone Trust It? — Michele Grant, Leading at Scale
summary: Michele Grant uses an illustrative acquisition-integration assistant to distinguish a working pilot from trustworthy operational autonomy. Her framework starts with baselines for reporting time, capacity, cost, and material-issue detection, then assigns operational ownership, risk oversight, and independent assurance. A documented human-work standard defines authority and escalation; decision logs and agent inventories preserve versions, dependencies, and evidence. Autonomy advances through shadow work, reviewed drafts, sampled exception handling, and more independent operation only when scorecard evidence supports it. At later stages, missed issues matter as much as alerts, and declining overrides may reflect weaker review rather than better performance. The scenario is explanatory, not a disclosed deployment outcome.

title: What Technical Due Diligence Finds When the Deck Says “70% Automated” — Soukaïna Abelhad
summary: Soukaïna Abelhad proposes technical-diligence checks for claims such as seventy percent automation. First compare workload growth with fully loaded human labor, including review, escalation, and rework. Next define whether automation means drafting, human approval, or genuine end-to-end completion within an explicit boundary. Finally inspect evaluation maturity: who labeled ground truth, whether domain experts agree with automated graders, and which bad outputs escaped. Examples show why benchmark passes and maintainer acceptance can diverge. Her preferred economic measure is cost per accepted autonomous task, including failures and human effort. The talk uses public and anonymous examples to structure diligence, not to establish a universal automation rate or causal explanation of company outcomes.

title: The Cost of Accessibility in AI — Jemima Abu, CAIS
summary: Jemima Abu examines the quality requirements that coding agents miss when accessibility is not explicit. A small uncontrolled comparison finds an accessibility skill producing a design faster and at lower cost, but she cautions that one experiment cannot establish a general cost advantage. The broader argument is that inaccessible code teaches agents poor conventions, while native HTML can avoid verbose custom behavior. She recommends defining accessibility requirements from the business and design stages, auditing the existing interface, using reusable patterns and explicit agent skills, and testing keyboard and assistive behavior. Automated checks help, but human testing remains necessary; accessibility is a property of the finished experience, not proof supplied by a prompt.

title: What a $900M Bank Error Teaches Us About AI Agents - John Feminella, Two Sigma
summary: John Feminella uses Citibank’s mistaken Revlon payment to show how formal procedures and several approvers can still permit a catastrophic outcome. His proposed agent-control architecture combines automatic registration, risk-sensitive review, purpose-linked tool permissions, shared firm-wide evaluation infrastructure, and conservative classifiers for routine action decisions. The evaluation section treats model changes as runtime-dependency changes that require regression tests, while shared tooling handles common evaluation mechanics so each team can specify what should hold for its own agent. Deterministic rules cover clear cases and human review focuses on ambiguous or consequential actions. The talk emphasizes usable controls that preserve iteration rather than blanket approval queues or unverified autonomy.

title: Lessons from Trillion Token Deployments at Fortune 500s — Alessandro Cappelli, Adaptive ML
summary: Alessandro Cappelli argues that production AI requires a feedback-driven lifecycle rather than stopping at a convincing demonstration. Within an RL-focused presentation, he explains how existing or mocked agent environments generate trajectories, while execution checks, business outcomes, and LLM judges define success. Human involvement shifts toward specifying rubrics and realistic scenarios, including difficult customer interactions. The Q&A distinguishes using a small set of early judgments to refine prompted evaluators from using larger production-feedback collections to train reward models. He also discusses implicit feedback as use-case-dependent. These are proposed practices for integrating quality signals into training, not a demonstrated comparative study of judge reliability.

title: Why More Context Makes Your Agent Dumber and What to Do About It — Nupur Sharma, Qodo
summary: Nupur Sharma explains why larger context windows do not eliminate attention failures or unproductive agent orchestration. She compares retrieval, summaries, graphs and critic loops, then describes Qodo’s specialized review agents and a judge that combines their findings with relevant code and prior PR context. Validation is more constrained than exploration, and accepted or rejected recommendations influence subsequent weighting. Audience questions probe whether historical behavior is an appropriate quality standard and how explicit security or compliance rules should override learned preferences. The talk’s evaluation relevance lies in contextual judging, feedback quality and the limits of treating acceptance as correctness.

title: Teaching LLMs to Speak Spotify — Yves Raimond & Jacqueline Wood, Spotify
summary: Spotify’s speakers describe an LLM-native recommendation system and the evaluation work needed to support it. Their NEO recipe adds semantic catalog tokens, grounds them with a frozen backbone, and then performs multitask instruction tuning. Ablations compare retained language ability, task performance and decoding tradeoffs. The evaluation section explains why interaction metrics alone cannot judge intent alignment or explanation quality. Grounding judges with textual listening profiles produced reported 75% alignment with human preferences; behavioral examples particularly helped ambiguous search queries. Grounded judges also replace expensive human ranking in pooled evaluation collections, with reported agreement of 0.87 on system rankings.

title: Build a Research Agent with Claude Managed Agents (Part 2 of 4) — Anthropic
summary: Priyanka Phatak and Gabe Cemaj build a research application on Claude Managed Agents, adding event-stream chat, SEC EDGAR skills, subagents, custom tools, and shared memory. The evaluation-relevant feature is Outcomes: a task and rubric drive a separate grading step that sends the agent back to work when the requested result is not yet satisfied, within configured bounds. A Nvidia research example illustrates a scorecard and verifier alongside specialist analysis agents. Q&A examines grading placement, guardrails, credential handling, and memory. The demonstration connects managed orchestration to explicit completion criteria, but self-supervision still depends on the rubric and grader rather than proving that a financial conclusion is independently correct.

title: Why Humans Can't Keep Up With AI-Written Code - Tariq Shaukat, Sonar
summary: Tariq Shaukat argues that agentic software production needs quality engineering rather than a larger human-review queue. He uses manufacturing analogies and cited studies to describe review overload, automation bias, declining performance on large codebases, compounding errors in long tasks, and instability in LLM judges. His proposed code-confidence framework combines intent, guardrails, independent verification, and evidence. Verification should be layered, address different failure classes, and produce actionable findings rather than merely collect another approval. The talk reports customer and survey observations, but its transferable point is methodological: increased code generation does not establish increased safe delivery, and self-assessment or nominal human oversight is insufficient evidence.

title: From Blind Spots to Merged PRs: Continuous Agentic Performance Optimization - May Walter, Hud
summary: May Walter describes a production workflow that turns runtime evidence into prioritized performance improvements. Scheduled agents correlate code with function-level traces, queries, latency, and forensic examples, then investigate likely high-ROI opportunities. Early failures included plausible but unverified diagnoses, complex-query mistakes, and superficial exception suppression. Skills and better production-to-code context made investigations more consistent, while rerun tests and runtime measurements established whether proposed fixes actually helped. Human-friendly reports, rather than floods of pull requests, rank opportunities by impact, risk, and business relevance. The adjacent evaluation lesson is that trustworthy automation must validate both the causal improvement and whether the issue deserves scarce review attention.

title: Morgan Stanley's ALPHALAB: Multi-Agent Research Across Optimization Domains — Brendan Rappazzo
summary: Brendan Rappazzo presents AlphaLab, Morgan Stanley's provider-agnostic harness for research, evaluation construction, and parallel experimentation. A strategist proposes experiments, workers implement and analyze them, and humans steer a shared board. The initial evaluation builder used separate conceptual and programmatic critics to catch leakage and code defects. Failures prompted a stricter second version: agents submit containerized models against public feedback, while users inspect held-out private validation. Rappazzo describes using carefully designed environments and qualitative research-process rubrics to optimize the harness itself and explore weight updates. He reports a top-12% Kaggle finish with limited iterations, while emphasizing that enterprise value lies in trustworthy evaluation environments and encoded expertise, not orchestration alone.

title: Reinforcement Learning without Verifiable Rewards — Will Brown, Prime Intellect
summary: Will Brown explains how to manufacture useful reinforcement-learning signals when real-world tasks lack clean correctness checks. He treats environments as reusable evaluation and training objects, grounding task generation in production traces, documents, and repositories. Working backward from known solutions can create solvable tasks, while controllable simulators provide checks unavailable in live systems. Model judges inspect completed trajectories, extract failure-specific rubrics, and support cheaper subsequent audits. Brown emphasizes searching for appropriately difficult tasks, probing reward hacking, and validating environments through small training runs. He also argues that continual learning needs supervised environmental knowledge alongside RL, with humans retaining authority over goals and consequential judgments.

title: Bringing Continual Learning into Enterprises — Samuel Denton, Applied Compute
summary: Samuel Denton organizes enterprise continual learning along two axes: offline versus online production traces, and static versus rollout-specific hints. Offline distillation targets known behaviors without replayable environments; online hinting supports an ongoing serving-and-training loop without requiring golden answers. He separates task-submission rate from underlying test success when teaching a coding agent to finish sooner, reporting submission improvement from about 22% to 60% without degraded test performance. Another example reports hyperlink-format compliance rising from roughly 15% to 80% with dynamic hints. Implementation lessons include selecting where to inject hints, distilling nearby steps, and using judge-selected relevant tokens to learn targeted behaviors while limiting broader capability degradation.

title: Prototyping as Leadership: How a CTO Ships with AI Agents
summary: Hursh Agrawal describes fitting agent-assisted prototyping into a CTO’s schedule, with a substantial example of overnight evaluation-driven optimization. Prototype feedback buttons save inputs, prompts and qualitative comments as JSON; the agent converts these examples into an evaluation set, collaborates with the human on scoring rubrics and builds a harness to hill-climb quality, latency and cost. He acknowledges overfitting risks with small datasets, although his proposed instruction to avoid overfitting is not a substitute for held-out validation. A second example delegates model-class comparisons and training for a PII classifier. Reliable CI, independent review, sandboxed infrastructure and morning human testing provide necessary organizational scaffolding.

title: Weight Folding, CUDA Streams, and the Bug That Made My Model Speak Backwards — Filip Makraduli
summary: Filip Makraduli explains FlashNorm, an RMS-normalization optimization using weight folding and parallel computation, then recounts a correctness failure that ordinary checks missed. Unit tests and perplexity looked acceptable, but longer generations revealed repetitions and a one-step lag. The cause was an implicit CUDA-stream join that let post-scaling read an unfinished buffer; explicit synchronization fixed it. He then discusses ablations of the proposed operations, compatibility with compiled and quantized models, and deploying modified checkpoints on open inference infrastructure. Its evaluation relevance is the gap between small tests or aggregate quality metrics and sustained generation behavior when low-level performance optimizations alter execution.

title: Robot Demos Are Easy. Reliability Is Hard — Jason Ma, Dyna Robotics
summary: Jason Ma explains how Dyna Robotics moves beyond attractive demonstrations toward sustained commercial task reliability.
