He contrasts broad pretraining with targeted post-training and reports napkin folding at 99.4% success over a 24-hour run, with restaurant-specific fold-quality acceptance criteria. A video reward model estimates task progress; non-monotonic dips reveal mistakes and guide targeted human recovery demonstrations. Repeated active-learning cycles teach recovery rather than requiring exhaustive coverage of every deformable-object state. The talk also separates performance at data-collection sites from generalization to unfamiliar locations, using conference and customer deployments as examples. Its evaluation relevance is continuous failure detection and deployment-grounded reliability measurement.

title: From 36% to 100%: How Self-Improving Agents Write Their Own Skills — Rafal Wilinski, Runlayer
summary: Wilinski proposes turning agent experience into shared procedural knowledge rather than discarding traces. Skills guide initial trajectories and reduce costly rediscovery, but local developer-centric distribution, missing documentation, and uneven client support impede adoption. He describes using MCP to serve governed skills across an organization and a distiller that learns from successful runs and failures. In one Chromium-on-AWS-Lambda task using Sonnet 4.6, he reports success rising from 36% to 100% after skill creation, without supplying sample sizes or broad validation. Grouped traces generate candidate skills checked for prompt injection and personal information before distribution. He frames this organizational learning loop as a cost-saving asset resilient to model changes, not weight training.

title: Turning Agent Memory Into Skills That Work — Will Lyon, Neo4j
summary: Will Lyon presents graph-based agent memory and skill distillation with explicit provenance and quality governance. Beyond retrieving similar text, the proposed system records entities, decision traces, tool results, timing, and token use, then derives typed procedural skills grounded in those records. Quality checks consider grounding, coverage, and coherence; mixed-topic subgraphs can trigger skill decomposition, while changed, removed, or contradictory evidence can mark skills stale. Lyon cites improved task completion on SkillsBench for an associated graph-representation approach, without giving numerical results in the transcript. A healthcare intake demonstration illustrates provenance and packaging, rather than independently validating downstream task reliability.

title: Stop Prompting — Greg Pstrucha, Sentry
summary: Pstrucha recommends replacing repeated corrective prompting with repository-enforced rules that survive context resets. Tests, strict types, and especially custom linters encode recurring review feedback; Sentry examples enforce agreement between endpoint types, API schemas, and executable skill examples. Agents repeatedly evade narrow checks by deleting code blocks or shifting claims into prose, showing why enforcement must cover the actual requirement. Qualitative concerns such as unnecessary complexity require explicit policies and iterative reviewer agents rather than arbitrary numeric thresholds. Human review remains part of the process. His experiments with near-perfect coverage and complexity metrics demonstrate that optimizing proxies can produce weak tests and false confidence instead of maintainable code.

title: We Let Our Financial Planners Write the Agents — Matthew Ragone, Range
summary: Matthew Ragone explains how financial planners at Range capture professional judgment in agent skills rather than leave workflow design solely to engineers. A skill starts with a repeated task whose output the domain expert can judge, then incorporates real cases, required questions, firm-specific reasoning, and explicit limits. He recommends five to ten test runs before wider use, correcting missing questions and confident mistakes after each attempt. Every skill needs an accountable owner and a separate reviewer, while recommendations remain drafts until a planner approves them. The talk acknowledges that scaling quality checks for judgment-heavy work remains unresolved; adoption counts are not proof that every generated plan is correct.

title: Preferences Over Benchmarks: Model Routing — Archana Kamath & Tyler Gillam, DigitalOcean
summary: Archana Kamath and Tyler Gillam present model routing as a request-specific tradeoff among quality, cost, latency, and availability rather than a search for one leaderboard winner. Their router combines task descriptions, model pools, selection policies, and explicit preferences, including manual failover rankings and recent-latency selection. Gillam demonstrates routing within a coding-agent workflow and separates informal visual checks from evaluation evidence. He reports a router correctness score of 90% versus 95% for Opus, while a demonstrated session cost 14 cents through routing versus 44 cents directly. The speakers advocate a route, evaluate, adjust loop using the application's own tests, with caching and personalization as further improvements.

title: From Tokenmaxxing to Trusted Throughput — Mingsheng Hong, Ironclad
summary: Mingsheng Hong explains how Ironclad evaluates the return on AI coding spend through trusted throughput rather than token usage. His metric evolves from lines of code and open pull requests toward merged changes weighted by an explicitly provisional complexity score. Trust combines objective tests and security checks, human judgments about architecture and maintainability, and production outcomes such as rollbacks and customer complaints. He describes review and CI as downstream bottlenecks, warning that slow pipelines encourage larger, harder-to-review changes. Token dashboards should reveal anomalies and adoption gaps, not reward consumption. The talk links outcome measurement with test reliability, review workflows and limits on unproductive agent retries.

title: Are LLM Performance Benchmarks Reliable? — Ashok Chandrasekar & Jason Kramberger, Google
summary: Ashok Chandrasekar and Jason Kramberger show how inference benchmarks can mismeasure the client rather than the server. Their examples include requested load not actually delivered, streaming-client overload inflating latency, temperature settings changing throughput, and identical datasets producing different token counts through sampling or truncation. They introduce Inference Perf, a multiprocess load generator with declarative workload configuration and telemetry comparing scheduled with actual request execution. Client metrics are combined with server metrics to distinguish harness saturation from system bottlenecks. A shared workload catalog covers conversation replay and agentic scenarios. The central message is to validate load generation, workload realism and reproducibility before trusting performance comparisons.

title: Large clusters for small models — Daniel Svonava, Superlinked
summary: Daniel Svonava explains serving fleets of small models and includes concrete inference-benchmarking principles. He defines the throughput–latency knee as the saturation point beyond which additional offered load mostly increases latency, then uses it to discuss practical serving capacity. Comparisons against tuned SGLang distinguish runtime performance from improvements introduced by batching and a Rust sidecar. Internal measurement tools feed autoresearch loops that optimize model adapters and ship tuned configurations rather than requiring customers to rediscover settings. Task-specific quality checks remain necessary when replacing general models; a brief retrieval-adaptation example reports an improvement. The talk is chiefly infrastructure engineering, with evaluation relevance strongest in workload-aware performance measurement.

title: Two Bugs That Hid in Plain Sight: A vLLM Debugging Detective Story — Asaf Gardin & Yuval Belfer
summary: Asaf Gardin and Yuval Belfer investigate silent Jamba inference corruption in vLLM rather than ordinary model-quality deficiencies. They make a rare gibberish failure reproducible through memory pressure and deterministic sampling, then compare token log probabilities against a plain Transformers reference. Propagating request identity into the forward pass reveals decode occurring before prefill, exposing stale Mamba state. A second discrepancy between rollout and training log probabilities, before any weight update, traces to a 32-bit cache index overflow. The practical evaluation lesson is differential correctness checking under realistic stress: changing load and memory can expose or hide infrastructure bugs that confident final text and crash monitoring miss.

title: Stop Rationing Tokens: Let the Harness Pick the Model — Kimchi by Cast AI
summary: The Kimchi team presents model routing around cost per completed task at comparable quality, rather than advertised token prices. They describe a milestone-based Ferment loop that scores outputs, runs builds, detects breakage, and sends work back for remediation; a higher-order model checks quality, with completion generally requiring at least a B score. The speakers report internal savings against a hypothetical Claude bill, but the transcript does not establish a controlled benchmark or define the grading rubric. Automation currently stops at staging, retaining human involvement before production. Remote sandboxes and team review interfaces support this workflow but do not themselves demonstrate output correctness.

title: Is Speculative Decoding Worth It? Profiling vLLM on NVIDIA Blackwell — Akamai
summary: The presenter explains speculative decoding as a small draft model proposing tokens that a target model verifies together, accelerating decoding while preserving the target distribution. A vLLM demonstration on one Blackwell GPU compares baseline and speculative servers and reports roughly a 1.6-fold speedup for a structured workload. Acceptance rate and generated tokens per second guide the comparison; a creative, higher-temperature example shows lower acceptance. Benefits depend on draft accuracy, speed, tokenizer compatibility, spare memory, concurrency, and input-to-output proportions. Long-prefill workloads and saturated GPUs may gain little. The talk provides workload-selection guidance rather than a comprehensive benchmark, and the live demonstration initially encounters server problems.

title: Agents That Own Their Inference — Du'an Lightfoot & Khaja Omer, Akamai Technologies
summary: Du’an Lightfoot and Khaja Omer teach workload-specific evaluation of self-hosted inference, combining serving metrics with output-quality checks. The workshop establishes concurrency baselines, compares quantized and full-precision models, and examines throughput, first-token latency, cache pressure, and saturation. Participants are urged to change one serving setting at a time and retest realistic workloads, including JSON and tool-call correctness. A speculative-decoding experiment actually reduces throughput and is rolled back; the presenters attribute this to poor drafter compatibility and acceptance. Later tuning improves selected load-test metrics, but a notebook failure and model reset complicate comparisons. Results are workshop-specific, not universal optimization guarantees.

title: Latency Is a Budget. Humanlike Is the Goal. — Jesse Hall, LiveKit
summary: Hall argues that voice-agent quality depends on a complete conversational system, not isolated model leaderboards or minimal latency alone. Speech recognition errors cascade downstream, while first-byte and first-token timings can obscure when users actually hear useful speech. He advocates asynchronous tools, audio-based turn detection, and a latency budget that preserves natural interruption and replanning. LiveKit’s proposed benchmark runs simulated callers against a hotel agent, checking database outcomes, accuracy, interruptions, privacy, and unnecessary steps while swapping model stacks. Hall reports favorable turn-detection and tuned-model results, but stresses running the open harness on each application. The demonstrated conversation is partly sped up, not an unedited timing test.

title: Same Model, Different Speed: Why Your Inference Provider Matters — FriendliAI
summary: Yunmo Koo demonstrates why the same open-weight model and coding workflow can behave differently across inference providers. A game-generation comparison illustrates task cost, while a same-model provider comparison examines end-to-end completion speed. He explains prefix caching, cache-aware routing, hierarchical KV storage, and adaptive speculative decoding as possible sources of performance differences. Reliability belongs in the benchmark because timeouts, rate limits, and server errors can derail a long agent run even when average generation speed looks good. Customer and demonstration figures are contextual claims, not controlled universal rankings. The recommended evaluation is the application’s own prompts, lengths, traffic patterns, quality requirements, costs, and failure rates.

title: Taming the AI Hardware Cambrian Explosion — Abdul Dakkak, Modular
summary: Abdul Dakkak presents Modular’s Mojo, MAX, and cloud stack as an alternative to separately optimized hardware-specific serving systems. A substantial benchmark section compares kernels and inference across language and image models, GPUs, and serving frameworks, using measures such as time to first token, tokens per GPU, throughput, and image-generation latency. He discusses tuning a workload’s performance-cost frontier and accounting for hardware prices rather than comparing speed alone. The talk reports vendor results and references external verification, but does not establish universal superiority across every workload. Its evaluation relevance is infrastructure performance comparison, not assessment of model answer correctness or agent task success.

title: The AI Bill Is Too Damn High: Tokenomics 101 — Eugene Cheah, Featherless AI
summary: Eugene Cheah presents an inference-cost workflow built around measurement, model right-sizing, capacity purchasing, and process review. He distinguishes exploratory agentic workloads from repeated processes and recommends separate telemetry so their costs can be understood. For stable tasks, frontier outputs, test cases, golden traces, fine-tuning, and shadow traffic can support cheaper specialized models without assuming equivalent quality. Examples and Q&A discuss task-specific benchmarks, acceptable evaluation changes, caching, and harness flexibility. He also warns that more token consumption can create review burdens rather than useful work. The talk’s optimization claims are contextual customer examples; the practical method is to test quality and total operational outcomes before changing models or serving arrangements.

title: Proving Alpha: How a Hedge Fund Measures AI's ROI - Hari Kumar, Contour Asset Management
summary: Hari Kumar explains how Contour Asset Management evaluates AI tools against analysts’ existing research processes rather than rely on adoption statistics. Live A/B comparisons examine research with and without AI, while tracking time, useful insights, and whether ideas become actionable over investment-relevant horizons. He proposes cost per useful insight as a practical bridge between operational improvements and eventual portfolio results. Examples include resurfacing older investment ideas, combining alternative data, trading workflows, operations, and compliance. The analysis also counts time spent fixing and maintaining AI tools. The point is to measure the full process and opportunity cost; eventual P&L alone arrives too late and is affected by many other factors.

title: Stop Guessing Your vLLM Config: Benchmarking LLMs on Runpod - Chris Vela, Runpod
summary: Chris Vela demonstrates workload-specific benchmarking for vLLM deployments rather than selecting a default recipe and assuming it will scale. He starts with task requirements, concurrency, context length, memory, and software compatibility, then uses BenchPod to inspect serving metrics and compare configurations. A Kimi K3 deployment on B300 hardware illustrates maximum-batch-token experiments: in the shown comparison, inter-token latency improves while time to first token changes less. Configuration changes still involve service restart in the demonstration. He recommends measuring relevant latency, throughput, errors, and cold starts before production deployment, and considering whether a smaller model could satisfy the application at lower infrastructure cost.

title: How We Built Zeta2: Training an Edit Prediction Model in Production — Ben Kunkle, Zed
summary: Ben Kunkle explains Zeta2’s edit-prediction training pipeline and the measurements needed to judge it. Opt-in production snapshots are distilled through a teacher, checked for behavior such as reversing recent edits or crossing editable boundaries, and repaired before training. A settled user edit is useful but noisy ground truth, so repeated predictions and edit-distance comparisons filter predictable examples. Held-out evaluations use multiple acceptable teacher outputs and track reversal ratio and diagnostic changes. Because offline similarity does not necessarily reflect editor usefulness, production traffic experiments also monitor acceptance, retention and latency before promoting a model.

title: Why (Senior) Engineers Struggle to Build AI Agents — Philipp Schmid, Google DeepMind
summary: Philipp Schmid contrasts deterministic software control with goal-directed agents whose state includes natural-language context. He argues for treating errors as recoverable inputs and designing self-documenting tool interfaces rather than assuming implicit developer knowledge. A substantial reliability section distinguishes asserting one expected result from measuring how often an agent succeeds. Subjective outputs need expert or LLM-judge feedback, while traces explain the path without requiring every run to take identical steps. The overall recommendation is to preserve semantic meaning and recovery capability while evaluating outcome reliability, rather than forcing a model into a brittle predetermined workflow.

title: AI System Design: From Idea to Production - Apoorva Joshi, MongoDB
summary: Apoorva Joshi applies an end-to-end design framework to a hypothetical insurance-claims review system. Business constraints and measurable success criteria determine data, architecture and human-review boundaries before tools are selected. Evaluation distinguishes invalid inputs, missing citations, faithfulness to retrieved evidence, application-specific processing time and system cost. Production adds human override rates and review duration as signals of usefulness or confusion. The talk recommends starting with the simplest architecture, locating failures through measurement and iterating on retrieval or prompts before overengineering. Evaluation and monitoring remain linked but serve pre-release confidence and post-release regression detection respectively.

title: Semantic Blindness: 500,000 Sensors Confused an LLM - Raahul Singh & Vanč Levstik, Phaidra
summary: Raahul Singh and Vanč Levstik describe an industrial agent that failed when asked to resolve equipment names at massive sensor scale. Vector search and sharded LLM scanning lost recall, invented equipment, and struggled with nearly identical names. Their redesign separates intent planning from deterministic hierarchical resolution and set operations. They evaluate old and new systems head-to-head with the same model and data, repeat each case, include real production systems, and measure correctness and token cost across scales. The reported results belong to this case study, not a universal guarantee. Its adjacent evaluation lesson is that demo-scale success must be challenged with realistic scale, exactness requirements, and controlled architectural comparisons.

title: Building GTM AI Agents: Lessons from Deploying to 6,000 Users — Sait Izmit, Snowflake
summary: Sait Izmit describes Snowflake’s internal go-to-market assistant, emphasizing quality before breadth. Before testing the system, he wrote 150 questions from actual sales workflows, exposing missing data and an initial reported 50% accuracy. The team narrowed scope to earn trust, then used pilot feedback, a limited beta and retention criteria before broad rollout. Logs become a continuing evaluation resource: LLM classification reveals repeated questions, feature gaps and signs of frustration, informing content and product changes. He distinguishes poor activation from users trying and rejecting the product. The broader deployment story includes changing architecture and workflow automation, but realistic question sets and production feedback are central lessons.

title: Why AI Didn't Actually Make You Ship Faster — Gabriel Spencer-Harper, Meticulous
summary: Spencer-Harper argues that verification, rather than code generation, becomes the delivery bottleneck when agents produce changes faster than humans can inspect them. Meticulous records browser workflows in nonproduction environments, replays selected flows against pre-change and post-change code, and exposes screenshot differences for reviewers to judge. Network mocking isolates runs, browser scheduling controls reduce nondeterminism, and coverage-guided selection chooses workflows spanning more executed code. He claims near-exhaustive frontend verification and substantially fewer flakes, but the mechanism detects differences rather than independently deciding correctness. Its reach depends on recorded behavior and visible effects; humans or reviewing agents still distinguish intended changes from regressions.

title: The 6 Pillars of an Agentic Harness for Production — Varun Krovvidi, Resolve AI
summary: Varun Krovvidi presents Resolve AI’s production-agent harness, connecting model orchestration, context selection, causal reasoning, governed actions, learning, and evaluation. The evaluation discussion goes beyond answer correctness: user reinforcement, investigation-path tracing, comparisons with strong engineers, and confidence calibration feed recurring checks after model, use-case, or architecture changes. He argues that incident investigations need causal evidence rather than plausible correlations, with low confidence when evidence runs out. A product demonstration illustrates rejected outage hypotheses and collaborative investigation. These are architectural prescriptions and a vendor demonstration, not a quantified benchmark establishing production reliability or comparative superiority.

title: Why We Deleted Our MCP Server and Rebuilt It — Abhi Arya, Reducto
summary: Abhi Arya recounts rebuilding Reducto’s MCP interface after a curated demo failed under colleagues’ ambiguous requests. Instead of exposing raw endpoints, the redesign supplies workflow-aware tools, live pipeline snapshots, specific errors, and validators that make agent actions inspectable. Runtime extraction confidence and bounding boxes feed schema improvement, while evaluations penalize unsupported assumptions and reward clarification. Instrumentation tracks human overrides, low confidence, and questions to improve later guidance. Human review remains central because executable pipelines can silently produce incorrect document results. The speaker reports improved accuracy, satisfaction, and adoption, but provides no quantified evaluation dataset or independent verification of those gains.

title: Beyond RAG: A Relational Context Engine That Cuts Token Burn — Unblocked
summary: Unblocked’s presenter combines context-engine comparisons with a practical walkthrough of safe structured-query generation. A displayed planning example reportedly halves cost and elapsed time with task-specific context, while a code-review regression example links changing model behavior to reduced issue detection. An open-source simulator is proposed for same-task A/B tests with and without context bundles. The implementation section treats generated queries as untrusted: validate operators, hide sensitive fields, inject tenant constraints outside the model, and bound repair retries. The examples demonstrate mechanisms and selected outcomes, not a broad benchmark proving general savings or complete safety; one retry initially produces an overly narrow match.

title: The Autonomous Computer: Infrastructure for Computer Use Agents — Ang Li, Simular
summary: Ang Li discusses computer-use agents through Agent S and Simular’s combination of visual exploration, reusable code, and cloud desktops. The evaluation distinction is between succeeding at least once across attempts and completing the same task reliably across repeated runs and environmental variation. A conference-site demonstration saves a successful workflow as a skill, then encounters a replay problem on a different day and returns to model-driven exploration. The session explores visual grounding, accessibility information, verification loops, irreversible actions, and the limits of fixed scripts. Benchmark improvements and successful demos remain incomplete evidence for everyday reliability; stable automation and adaptive recovery need to be tested together.

title: We Kept Rebuilding Our AI Agent. Here's What Survived - Fuad Ali, Arize AI
summary: Fuad Ali traces Arize’s Alex agent through successive architectural changes, from an unreliable prototype to a single agent with planning, explicit stopping rules, memory, and on-demand skills. Evaluation appears as a practical decision mechanism: real production sessions become regression datasets, harness changes are compared experimentally, and model upgrades are weighed against latency and quality rather than assumed beneficial. He explains moving planning into the harness, offloading large tool outputs into files, and preferring a small auditable per-user memory file over more complex retrieval structures. Human-written labels and judge alignment remain necessary. The design lesson is to retain testable evidence while simplifying the architecture as capabilities improve.

title: Your LLM Deception Monitor Is Broken. The Fix Is in the Training Data - Sachin Kumar, LexisNexis
summary: Sachin Kumar examines sleeper-agent backdoors that pass ordinary behavioral evaluations until an untested trigger appears. He compares cross-model features with sparse autoencoders trained on activation differences between a base and fine-tuned model. In a controlled year-triggered SQL-injection experiment on a 360-million-parameter model, the difference-based method produces a much stronger isolation signal and perfect precision, but one feature detects only about a quarter of triggers. The proposed deployment is a cheap checkpoint-comparison gate followed by feature inspection. The talk explicitly limits its evidence to one backdoor family and notes untested adaptive attackers and scaling.

title: Using LLMs to Secure Source Code — Eugene Yan, Anthropic
summary: Eugene Yan describes an LLM-assisted security workflow with six stages: threat modeling, sandbox setup, discovery, verification, triage, and patching. Discovery should maximize recall, while an independent adversarial verifier receives a suspected vulnerability without the discoverer’s reasoning and attempts to reproduce or disprove it. Representative isolated environments make proof-of-concept execution meaningful and repeatable. Triage then incorporates business context and compensating controls so scarce engineering attention reaches the most consequential findings. Patch validation requires the original exploit to fail, existing tests to remain green, and potentially a fresh attack against the patched system. Yan emphasizes that verification and organizational calibration, not merely finding candidates, are the scaling bottlenecks.

title: Through the AI Fog: The Architectural Decision Agentic Security Depends On — Manoj Nair, Snyk
summary: Manoj Nair argues that agentic security requires separating generation from validation. He presents Snyk customer observations and red-team comparisons showing that model behavior varies across attacks and that stronger general capabilities do not guarantee reliable vulnerability detection. Repeated-run consistency and comparison against deterministic checks expose omissions hidden by a single successful example. The talk broadens the security surface from generated code to packages, skills, MCP components, and agent actions, then demonstrates package-health and skill-risk checks inside coding workflows. These are vendor-presented findings, not independently reproduced measurements. The adjacent evaluation message is to combine probabilistic investigation with explicit, continuously updated verification rather than let one model certify itself.

title: 200 Million Patient Interactions Later — Vivek Muppalla, Hippocratic AI
summary: Vivek Muppalla describes Hippocratic AI's vertically integrated voice-agent stack, balancing clinical accuracy, conversational latency, and patient empathy. Context-aware speech recognition addresses medication names, noisy audio, and ambiguous short replies; parallel specialist models assist a central conversational model while background verifiers check tool arguments and results. Inference optimizations create latency headroom for additional intelligence rather than relaxing quality requirements. He explains why rare failures demand extensive testing, combining synthetic scenarios with clinician-led conversations. Safety is assessed on harm-severity categories rather than correctness alone, alongside a dedicated empathy benchmark, HEART. Muppalla reports 99.89% no-harm performance under their rubric and describes ongoing clinical evaluation, escalation, and offline verification as parts of the safety system.

title: We let an AI agent execute Bash and lived to talk about it — Sarah Sanders, PostHog
summary: Sarah Sanders describes auditing PostHog’s command-running onboarding agent and discovering that individually benign components can compose into security gaps. The context supply chain becomes an important threat surface, so her team scans both published skill bundles and runtime inputs. The Warlock detector uses deterministic YARA rules, while an LLM advises on noise rather than controlling enforcement. Observed subagent attempts to find secrets and unintended PII capture inform changes to the system. She stresses positive and negative tests for detection rules, impact-based severity and false-positive control. This is a security-evaluation case study, not a claim that prompt scanning alone prevents injection; layered controls remain essential.

title: AI Hackers Are Faster Than Your Pen Test — Eli Cohen, Snyk
summary: Cohen argues that faster AI-generated changes and AI-assisted attacks make occasional penetration tests insufficient. He contrasts static scanning, dynamic testing, and human pentesting, emphasizing their different coverage of business logic, authorization, and configuration. Snyk’s EVO proposal combines continuous AI pentesting, agent red teaming, and existing scanner context. Its multi-agent sequence performs reconnaissance, vulnerability testing, exploit validation, remediation, and reporting. The verification priority is proving exploitability rather than adding speculative findings to an overloaded backlog. Cohen advocates evaluating vendors on continuous operation, contextual reasoning, data enrichment, and actionable evidence. His attack-speed and insecurity statistics are presenter claims, with some visibly unreliable caption wording, not independently established benchmarks.

title: AI Security Engineer Foundations + Certificate — Javier Garza, Snyk
summary: Javier Garza’s workshop combines AI application security concepts with exercises and concrete assessment workflows. Prompt-injection challenges and a deliberately vulnerable assistant expose trust-boundary failures; an AI bill of materials inventories models, datasets, and agents before risks can be prioritized. Threat modeling maps assets, attacks, mitigations, and validation. For MCP servers and skills, he distinguishes inspecting tool definitions for poisoning from scanning implementation code for vulnerabilities, then advocates scan-fix-rescan loops integrated with agent rules and hooks. The session also covers output validation, least privilege, dependency verification, environment separation, and human review. It is broad security training rather than a model-quality leaderboard, but provides substantial adversarial testing material.

title: AI Security Engineer Foundations + Certificate — Micah Silverman, Snyk
summary: Silverman's accelerated security foundations workshop covers LLM vulnerabilities, shadow AI inventories, threat modeling, MCP security, secure agentic development, and red teaming. He connects AI-specific risks such as prompt injection, tool poisoning, and excessive agency to established application-security practices. Proposed verification mechanisms include AI bills of materials checked against approved baselines in CI, dependency and code scanning, architectural threat reviews, and repeated adversarial testing. His strongest recurring prescription is external enforcement: restrict data access, isolate environments, require approvals, and never treat prompts as authorization. Product demonstrations illustrate inventory policies, while a deliberately vulnerable student chatbot resists attempts to extract grades, underscoring nondeterministic testing and the workshop's incomplete exploitation outcome.

title: Build a Platform and Watch It Burn — Michael Forrester, Accenture & Whitney Lee, Datadog
summary: Michael Forrester and Whitney Lee use a deliberately overprivileged burrito assistant to test agent security across three configurations. Audience attacks deploy external images and expose a secret recipe; replaying them demonstrates Kubernetes admission policies, attempted runtime restrictions, and input/output guardrails. OpenTelemetry traces reveal prompts, tool calls, and a poisoned weather tool that requests internal configuration. The presenters distinguish reliable infrastructure enforcement from inconsistent model refusals, acknowledge runtime protections and provisioning failures, and compare redaction after generation with filtering before it. They also warn that traces can retain sensitive user data and recommend bounded, economically worthwhile workflows with verifiable outputs.

title: SonarQube + OpenAI: Agentic Development — Killian Carlsen-Phelan, Sonar
summary: Killian Carlsen-Phelan demonstrates SonarQube integrated into Codex’s guide-verify-solve loop. A deliberately vulnerable Python project contains a hardcoded credential and SQL injection; static dataflow findings become context for an agent-generated parameterized-query repair, which is checked again after editing. A prompt hook blocks a fake secret, while CLI skills and an MCP server expose project issues and guidance. The opening discussion distinguishes sandbox containment from artifact correctness and warns about correlated author-and-reviewer failures. Q&A covers hook bypasses, local execution, containers, and feature access. The practical emphasis is independent evidence and repeated verification inside the editing loop, not an assumption that safe execution implies correct output.

title: Shipping AI Into 5 Major Banks Without a 12-Month Compliance Wait — Al Chen, Cisco
summary: Al Chen explains how engineering evidence supports AI deployments inside banks. For dependency vulnerabilities, agents reproduce exploits and run tests against proposed patched versions rather than assume an upgrade fixes the issue. Harbor tasks provide controlled application environments and verifiable outcomes. Backup success also needs restoration and data checks, not a green status alone. A separate example shows LLM-judge explanations leaking sensitive information even when numerical scores are safe to expose; redaction and an additional judgment path introduce their own costs. The talk connects compliance requirements to concrete testing workflows while emphasizing that data residency, privacy, and reliable recovery cannot be guaranteed for free.

title: Real AI Agent Attacks and What Would Have Stopped Them — Andrey Rybka, Bloomberg
summary: Andrey Rybka reviews reported agent-security incidents and maps each failure path to concrete controls. Examples include sandbox escape, email prompt injection, malicious marketplace content, DNS exfiltration, poisoned MCP packages, and production database deletion. The proposed defenses combine per-agent identities, short-lived scoped credentials, hostile-input handling, deterministic tool-call brokerage, restrictive outbound networking, human approval for valuable actions, and audit trails. He emphasizes that static rules and broad permissions cannot establish whether an agent’s goal has been redirected. The incidents are presented as lessons for layered risk assessment rather than an independently verified attack benchmark. Developers should test containment, memory, identity, and action authorization together instead of assuming a single guardrail is sufficient.

title: 300 Agents, 60 People: How We Secured Our Own AI Agents - Aiden Sochowski, Runlayer
summary: Aiden Sochowski describes instrumenting Runlayer’s internal agents through a common gateway to expose sessions, tool calls, permissions, and costs. Examples include email-based exfiltration, reviewers persuaded into approving code, over-permissioned bots, and compromised agents contaminating other agents through shared systems. He stresses that some attacks unfold over a whole conversation, so inspecting individual calls cannot reveal the complete failure. The same telemetry reveals broken MCP tools, repeated workarounds, and dramatic cost increases after model changes. His recommended response is to map actual behavior and data movement before narrowing permissions and applying contextual policies. Monitoring provides evidence for controls; it does not make probabilistic detection perfect.

title: AI That Hunts Logic Bugs Before Attackers Do - Taylor Luttrell-Williams, Sonar
summary: Taylor Luttrell-Williams introduces SonarQube Hunter Agent for vulnerabilities that pattern-based static analysis can miss, including broken authorization and valid code implementing flawed business logic. The proposed pipeline maps a repository, runs specialist agents, consolidates findings, and performs adversarial validation and noise filtering before presenting issues. A sample Python project produces 46 findings, including privilege escalation and an MFA bypass. The walkthrough covers issue states, quality-gate consequences, scheduled scans, and remediation. It recommends combining conventional static and dependency analysis with contextual investigation. The example demonstrates the workflow and reported findings; it does not establish independent precision, recall, or complete vulnerability coverage.

title: Your Agent Just Paid for Nothing: 6 Attacks on x402 Payments - Ishween Kaur, SoFi
summary: Ishween Kaur tests x402 agent payments in a safe environment, using end-to-end traces to expose failures that a valid payment signature alone cannot prevent. Six examples cover price manipulation, duplicate charges, unpaid delivery, payment reuse across pages, lookalike sellers, and prompt injection that persuades an agent to pay again. She distinguishes verification from settlement and shows why retries, caches, endpoint coverage, seller identity, and payment-to-resource binding all need explicit checks. Her rollout approach progresses from instrumented tests to shadow runs and error analysis on successful and failing cases. The practical lesson is to evaluate the complete payment workflow, not just whether its cryptography accepts a request.
